Summary
The agents take the elevator up to Ben’s office. Ben’s voice calls through the door. You two are back? Thank the Wings. He unlocks it.
He looks paler and weaker than before. No one has been bringing him anything without Dux’s orders. He gestures for them to sit.
First things first. Have you got the medicine? How are you doing? Burr explains that Koller could not find any visible bleeding. The machine might be malfunctioning.
Ben’s brow furrows. They discuss the possibility of Koller treating them for free. Ben listens. The conversation turns to the axe-man. Burr explains the checkpoint massacre. Ben looks troubled — that is not what Dux told him.
They discuss Dux. The prisoner committed suicide. Ben accuses Dux. But Dux could have killed Ben anytime. Why is Ben still alive? Ben struggles with the contradictions, his hands on his temples. He is not the president. He just wanted to give back.
Pug slides the vacuum-sealed bread across the table. Ben does not grab for it until it is halfway, missing his first grab. He opens the package and the bread poofs out. He cannot believe it. You boys are my saviors.
Burr gives Ben a half-eaten tin of oats. Ben thanks them.
They discuss the mechanic’s workshop key. Ben does not know its exact location, but has a good idea. The mechanic was the founder’s closest friend. The key would be either at the mechanic’s apartment — east, in uncontrolled territory — or the Founder’s apartment — west, on the other side of Death’s Head territory, controlled by a small syndicate known as the Brotherhood of Iron.
Ben gives them the addresses and approximate routes. He wishes them well.

Summary
A checkpoint with five guards ahead — three thugs and two bikers. One biker spots them, waves, then freezes. Two of the thugs have skeletal metal prosthetic arms. One biker has similar solid metal arms. They recognize the Death’s Head outfit. Fear spreads.
The skeleton-armed thug steps forward, hand outstretched. Burr swings the baseball bat without warning, cracking it across his temple. He crumples, the metallic arms clanging on the asphalt.
The augmented biker charges, tire iron swinging. Burr thrusts the bat like a rapier toward his throat — the man twists, catching it on his metal arm. Pug joins with the PVC pipe spear, slicing the biker’s cheek. The remaining thugs attack with a pool cue and a wrench. Burr swings upward, catching one under the chin. The augmented biker lands a blow on Burr’s helmet — the helmet absorbs the worst. Burr charges, grabbing the biker’s face, fingers pushing into his eyes, hooking into his mouth. He grabs the jaw and pulls. Dislocated. Fatal.
The other thugs flee. The remaining biker backs away and runs.
Burr examines the dead biker’s augment — arms replaced at the shoulders, metal plates across the back. He saws with the bread knife. The metal meets bone. The teeth grate but cannot cut through.
Just under twenty Death’s Head reinforcements round the corner. Ten thugs, four bikers, two armored bikers, two bouncer-types, and a woman leading — Jodi. The agents abandon the body and flee through the checkpoint into Brotherhood territory.

Summary
The agents arrive at the mechanic’s apartment building. Kurt sits behind the front desk, dozing. Dirk reads a magazine in the lobby — he is the escort. They are new faces here.
Burr describes Ben to gain entry. Kurt considers, then makes an exception. Dirk will accompany them upstairs.
The apartment is remarkably lived-in but dust-covered. Points of interest: closets and cabinets, a rug under the coffee table, a vase by the entrance, a bedroom vent, an empty picture frame, the bathroom.
Burr lifts the vase — a keyring with two keys falls out. Pug searches the kitchen drawers — AA batteries, a flashlight, and a pair of locked cabinets. The clean key opens the right cabinet: two rolls of duct tape, a can opener, a bundle of cloth. The taped key opens a bedroom closet safe: a packet of pills, a bundle of cash, a Swiss army knife. The left cabinet, opened with the clean key, yields tools: a plumbing wrench, a carpentry hammer, a pry bar.
Pug unscrews the vent. Inside: a glass bottle of murky white liquid (gasoline with a chemical smell) and two metal cans, welded shut. Burr pries open the floorboard — a lockbox requires a key. The bathroom sink pipe has a blockage: a black plastic ball wrapped in rubber bands. Inside: a tiny key.
The tiny key unlocks the floor lockbox. Inside: an M9 Bayonet with a black blade, lying atop a faded picture.
Pug examines the empty picture frame on the wall. He turns it over. A key is taped to the back.
The picture shows three men: the scruffy founder, the mechanic, and a younger Ben — all wearing the same corporate suits the agents woke up in.
They gather the loot, restore the apartment as best they can, and head downstairs. Kurt asks if they found what they were looking for. They did. He wishes them luck.
Outside, they notice a building with an unlit neon sign: G.W. — the G shaped like a shield, the W made of blades.

Past an alley, the sound of metal on metal. Burr breaks off the path. A one-sided fight: a full-body prosthetic cyborg with a chainsaw sword is being cornered by three men in clean jackets with baton-swords. Zuge of Neul’s Office, Grade 8 Fixer.
The agents pretend to side with the Fixers, circling behind. At the signal, they turn — Burr liver-kicks his target, Pug stabs his in the shoulder with the bayonet. The cyborg capitalizes, disarming his opponent.
The cyborg’s core overloads. His eyes glow, electricity arcs through him. He raises his arms, the unstable core clattering, light shining through cracks in his metal shell. The Fixers dive for cover. The agents follow.
The explosion tears through the alley. Shrapnel flies. One Fixer is hit badly. The cyborg’s upper torso disintegrates. Pug rolls aside as a massive metal arm crashes where he lay. Burr finds the chainsaw sword in the garbage — damaged, the trigger does nothing.
Zuge picks himself up, checks his wounded colleague, and drags him away.

Burr and Pug head back toward Death’s Head territory. The checkpoint where they killed the augmented guards is now reinforced with more personnel. Burr slaps the damaged chainsaw sword — it remains inert. A biker without a helmet, a red bandana covering his face, steps forward. Brick, sergeant-at-arms of the Death’s Head, subordinate of Road Captain Jodi.
Brick offers a deal: drop their gear and meet the bosslady, or be beaten and taken in. Burr refuses. Brick cracks his neck, pulls down his bandana. A faded purple-tinted tattoo travels down his eye and chin. He puts up his guard in a boxing stance.
The fight is brutal. Jab and counter. Feint and block. Brick’s tattoos begin to glow — a faded neon. His punches gain force. A heavy blow to Burr’s gut makes him vomit. Brick takes a black eye and a fractured clavicle. A final powered punch rocks Burr in the face, knocking him down. Brick stands over him, steam rising from burnt tattoos, blood dripping from his mouth.
Burr offers to turn himself in. Only himself. Not Pug.
Pug runs. Burr strikes at passing thugs, causing confusion and slowing the pursuit. He is tackled and pinned. Through the bodies holding him down, he sees Brick give a weak thumbs up before falling unconscious.

Pug runs. Through twisting alleys, unfamiliar territory, Death’s Head pursuers closing in. He tries doors — locked. Again — locked. Finally, one opens. He slams it behind him.
The building is a pawn shop. Knick-knacks line shelves. An elderly man stands behind the counter. Another customer occupies the shop — a shorter figure in a wide-brimmed hat, a large case on their back like an instrument case.
The pawnbroker greets him. Everything is for sale. Pug offers to pay for hiding. The pawnbroker demands fifty thousand. Pug grabs him, slams his head on the counter, draws his gun. The pawnbroker pleads to the other customer.
A loud thud. The customer drops their case. A young woman with short black hair stands revealed — a half-ceremonial robe adorned with velcro straps and zippers. She cocks her head. Are you an evildoer?
She sees through the pawnbroker’s lies. She offers to pay. The pawnbroker demands fifty thousand. She opens a pouch — two thousand. Will this work? The pawnbroker, intimidated, lowers his price to ten thousand. Pug agrees.
He hides in the back room — a cramped storage closet. The Death’s Head arrive. The pawnbroker sells him out. The woman is implicated too.

Kurisu grabs her case mid-sentence. She dropkicks the biker, sending him crashing into the other two. Spinning the case like a battering ram, she launches the biker through the shattered storefront window. The shop falls silent.

Pug leaves the pawn shop but quickly realizes he is lost. The unfamiliar streets all look the same. He backtracks to the pawn shop. Kurisu is still there, trying to right overturned shelves. The pawnbroker has disappeared. She looks up, surprised to see him back so soon.
Pug asks for directions. Kurisu pulls folded notes from a pouch — directions to her office’s lodging. She offers to lead him there herself. Despite her hesitation about leaving the mess, she decides helping him escape the evildoers is more important.
She leads him into the maze of alleys. A dead end. She studies the wall, reads the notes, looks up. This should not be here. She turns around, more careful this time. Another dead end. She hands the notes to Pug.

She insists she can get them back without the notes, with complete confidence. She leads on, choosing alleys at random, unfazed. Kurisu hands Pug a small Book, Notepad for copying the directions.

Burr awakens in a small, dark room. He is seated, slumped atop a chair, wrists bound behind him with thin plastic zip ties digging into his skin. A metal table sits in front of him. A glass wall to the left. A security camera to the right. An interrogation room.
The door opens. A tired man in Death’s Head attire enters. A baseball cap on his bald head. A clipboard tucked under his arm. Two plastic cups of water in his hands. He sits, sets the cups down, and avoids eye contact. He flips through pages. He glances at Burr from his peripheral. Finally, he slides the other cup forward.
The conversation stalls. The man has no questions ready. Burr begins dislocating his shoulder to free his hands — popping the joint out of its socket. The man returns with a manila folder, sees Burr mid-dislocation, and simply says “Oh. Alright, keep on then.” He sits back down and reads through the folder while Burr finishes the maneuver.
The water has powdery granules settled at the bottom. The man sips it himself. Just dirt.
The interrogation begins. The man places CCTV photos on the table: Burr cutting up the augmented Death’s Head member. The destroyed checkpoint. The clinic. Burr running from the clinic. Burr answers honestly — he was dying, he needed medicine.
The man asks about Koller. Burr confirms contact. The man lights up, scribbling notes excitedly. Thank you for your cooperation. He begins to leave.
Burr stops him. Offers a bargain: Stray Dog intel in exchange for his life. The man pauses. He can get Jodi. He leaves.

The tired interrogator returns with a woman. A casual button-up shirt hanging open over a tank top. Jeans. Combat boots. Shoulder-length wild hair, slightly reddish-brown. She wears no Death’s Head patches.
She saunters in, sits down without ceremony, and kicks her feet up on the table. Jodi. Road Captain of the Death’s Head.
Burr begins talking. He describes the Stray Dogs. Where they come from. Who they are out of costume. Their delivery routes. What they take. How they handle armed groups. Jodi listens without interrupting.

Summary
The tired interrogator unlocks the rusted doors of the Death’s Head Pound — a repurposed school. He shoves Burr forward. The doors slam shut behind him. The hallway is dark and silent, footsteps echoing off the tiles. A pile of clothes lies ahead. Two open classroom doors flank the hall.
Two inmates step out of the darkness into the hallway. One jeers — “Oi. Drop your shit. And you won’t die in here.”
Burr dashes forward before the second man can finish his taunt. He kicks forward into the man’s knee with unrestrained ferocity — the joint breaks out of place, bending backwards, crushed bone and screams as the inmate collapses, unable to support himself. Burr pivots and lunges for the other, grabbing him by the face and driving him down toward the floor. The back of the man’s head crashes into the tile. The sound of a splatter hitting Burr’s ankles. The first inmate continues screaming and writhing until Burr stomps down onto his head. Silence.
Burr continues down the hallway. He hears shuffling from a classroom on his right. He enters.
A man lies in the corner, half-reclining against the wall. Completely naked, save for an unfolded newspaper draped over him like a blanket. Short blonde hair. An eyepatch. Sleeping peacefully.
Burr rears his foot back to launch a kick at his head. Right before the apex of the wind-up, the man’s eye opens. Burr’s foot soars toward him — the man does not panic. His head tilts slightly in concern, and at the last moment, Burr’s foot crashes into the wall. The man’s head is now right beside where it was aimed.
“Good morning. Is that how people greet each other in here?”
The man does not know who he is or where his clothes are. Those two men took them. And his best friend. He killed people too — that is why he is here. He thanks Burr for his help and heads into the hallway to check the pile of clothes. They are not his. He heads off to search the classrooms near where the men came out, looking for his belongings.

Burr continues through the school. He reaches a T intersection — dark hallway to the left, light peeking from beneath a closed classroom door to the right. Jeering and laughter echo through the walls. He opens the door.
Four men sit around a small battery-powered lamp. The smell of cheap booze wafts through the air. Cans and bottles litter the floor around them. A large-bearded man laughs at a story.
Burr picks up an empty glass bottle at his feet. He charges forward and smashes it over the head of the nearest man — he crashes to the floor, the broken bottle becoming a jagged shard in Burr’s grip. Without pause, Burr sinks the broken bottle into the next man’s neck. Blood gurgles from his throat as he topples.
A desk helps with the third man — Burr hefts it like a club and swings it into the man’s head, the desk crashing down over him.
The bearded man is tougher. They exchange blows. The man headbutts Burr. A glass bottle thrown by one of the downed men smacks Burr square on the bridge of the nose, shattering. The man Burr stabbed with the desk gets up and tackles him into the wall. A desk leg stabs into Burr’s back but fails to penetrate. Burr tears out the bearded man’s beard. A bottle glances off Burr’s head. Burr shoves a fistful of broken glass into the bottle-throwing man’s mouth and drives an uppercut through his jaw.
The fight narrows to Burr and the bearded man. Burr goes for a groin strike — his knee meets something hard and metal in the man’s pants. Burr double palm-strikes his sternum, cracking something within. The bearded man falls back into a desk, the legs breaking beneath him. He yammers on from the floor. Burr shoves a bottle into his mouth and brings his heel down, driving it through.

Burr wanders through the halls. A light shines down the corridor. Ahead, four empty rooms, then one with light spilling from the doorway. He steps in something wet — blood.
Inside the room, splatters of blood decorate the walls like abstract art. A man stands over a body, his combat boot resting on its throat. He is well-built, wearing a black tank top and an empty chest rig. A black one-hole ski mask covers his face.
He looks up. “I’ve got no friendship for you murdering cocksuckers.” He studies Burr — the fresh blood splattered across him. Burr explains himself. The man is guarded but relents. “Alright, tough guy. Take point. Let’s see how you hold up.”
He retrieves a large combat knife from one of the bodies and sheathes it on his thigh. They head out together. Passing the room where Burr killed the four men, the ski-mask man nods in approval. “Clean wetwork. Didn’t leave anyone.”
Burr calls out for the eyepatch man. No reply. They find a thug writhing on the floor, his arm broken — the eyepatch man did this and went upstairs. Burr kicks the thug in the face, knocking him back, then stomps on his neck. Quiet.
Upstairs, a fur-collared thug sits against the wall, groaning. He laughs and spits at them. The ski-mask man lends his combat knife to Burr — handle first. Burr threatens the man, who points toward the broadcasting room. Satisfied, Burr drives the knife upward, through the man’s jaw and into his brain. He hands the knife back.
They head toward the broadcasting room.

Summary
Burr and the ski-mask man reach the broadcasting room. A red carpet lies before the door. A “LIVE” sign glows above it. Burr opens the door.
Inside, the room has been converted into a makeshift club — desks pushed together to form a grand table. The eyepatch man is already here, a varsity jacket tied around his waist. He stands across from several thugs in ratty fur coats. One holds his arm uselessly at his side. Four more are armed: an iron bar, a scrap metal machete, a pair of brass knuckles, and a security baton.
Behind them, behind the glass of the broadcasting studio, sits the Pound Boss — a large man in a tiger-striped fur coat. He leans back in an office chair, cigar in hand, watching. He opens a case and begins injecting himself with three syringes of colored liquid.
The eyepatch man does his warm-up stretches. The ski-mask man draws his knife.
The baton thug charges Burr. He crashes the baton into Burr’s side. Burr locks his leg around the man’s arm, seeking to break it. They tumble to the floor, the impact knocking the wind out of Burr. The man scrambles up, putting distance between them. Burr closes again, trapping him against a desk. A flurry of jabs and punches — the man has augmentations, absorbing blow after blow. But the damage accumulates. Burr grabs his head, mounts his chin, and yanks — a clean neck snap. The baton clatters to the floor.
Burr picks up the fallen baton. The brass knuckles thug rushes him. Burr thrusts the baton like a rapier, catching the man across the forehead. A moment of stagger. Burr swings down on the center of his skull — a spray of blood from the nose, jaw slack, the man crumpling forward. Burr catches him with a knee to the face, sending him sprawling over the other bodies.
Burr bends down and picks up the brass knuckles from the fallen thug’s hand. Worn metal, knicks and scratches across the surface.
The ski-mask man dispatches the iron bar thug with a knife to the solar plexus and repeated blows to the wall. He takes a machete to his forearm fighting the next thug, but uses the lodged blade to close the distance and delivers a relentless series of stabs.

The broadcasting room clears. Three dead thugs on the floor — the ski-mask man finishing the last of them. The eyepatch man stretches his arms, limbering up. Behind the glass, the Pound Boss stands. His tiger-striped fur coat hangs open. Three empty syringes lie at his feet.
He steps through the door into the main room. His muscles bulge and twitch — the serums working through his system. He cracks his neck and grins.
Burr and the ski-mask man advance together. The eyepatch man circles. The fight is brutal — the boss is augmented, faster and stronger than any thug they have faced. Blows that would kill a normal man only stagger him. But the numbers advantage tells. Burr closes, brass knuckles catching the boss across the jaw. The ski-mask man drives his knife deep. The eyepatch man lands a kick that buckles the boss’s knee.
The boss falls. The eyepatch man finishes him.
The eyepatch man retrieves his best friend from behind the boss’s desk — a compound bow wrapped in ragged cloth atop a stack of boxes. He holds it for a moment, checking it over. He looks at Burr. “We are friends, right?”
He leads Burr to a storage closet off the broadcasting room. Inside: a dark grey cloth cloak hangs from a hook. A nailgun with seven nails sits on a shelf beside it. A plexiglass riot shield leans against the wall. Take them. He nods toward the shield. The eyepatch man hides his compound bow behind a loose ceiling panel in the closet, covering it with his tarp. Waiting for a quieter time.
The ski-mask man is gone. The eyepatch man stays behind.
Burr is alone again. Equipped. The Pound is behind him.

Summary
Pez crosses the street toward the remaining Death’s Head guard. The guard spots him — a short figure in a tactical tunic approaching — and demands he stop. Pez gives a chipper, unbothered reply. The guard draws a lead pipe and threatens to take him to the station. Pez points across the street: “My friend over there said I need to talk to the man in the alleyway.”
The guard’s attention shifts to Pug. He raises his pipe. Pez slips into the alleyway, leaving Pug alone with the guard.
Pug plays the part. Distraught. Confused. Crying. The guard hesitates — lowers his pipe and approaches to detain rather than fight. He grabs Pug by the collar.
Pug grabs his ankles and yanks. The guard’s feet fly out from under him. He crashes onto his back, the air knocked out of his lungs. Pug draws a knife and presses it to his throat.
The guard freezes. He talks. The holding areas are past the station — old storage units converted into housing. He points in the direction Dust was taken. Pug drives the butt of his knife into the back of the guard’s head, knocking him out cold. He drags the body to a nearby dumpster, heaves him inside, and drops the lid.
Pez emerges from the alleyway. “Hello! I didn’t know I’m your son. Also, you’re really good at crying!” He got everything from the drunk guard — there are three different holding spots. One of them is an abandoned school. The Pound.
The two of them head down the street. They pass the alley where the drunk guard sits, back against the wall, eyelids heavy. He gives a friendly wave. Pez waves back. “Drink some water when you’re home!”

Summary
Pug and Pez follow the directions toward the Death’s Head station. As the building comes into view in the distance, a hushed voice calls out from an alleyway: “Hey! Psst! Over here dimwit!”
Kent, Kurisu, and Dust are waiting. Dust has their cowl and goggles back on. Kurisu sits atop her case. A beaten, gagged, tied-up guard lies face-down behind them, Dust perched on his back.
Kent squats beside the guard and tears the rag out of his mouth. She unloads: “Listen up chump, I’m here on business. I’m looking for my client — in one of your holding facilities. Spill the layout. Patrols. Numbers. Arms. Alarms. Security systems. Talk.”
The guard stares blankly. “Wh-what…?”
Kent punches him in the face. He goes limp.
Pez speaks up. “Yup! He told me there’s three different spots they hold prisoners. He was really helpful.” Pug confirms it — the drunk guard was forthcoming. Kent’s expression cycles through shock, mortification, and frustration.
“Why the fuck did you want me to interrogate this shithead then if you already knew where to go?”
She huffs, stands, and tells Pez to lead the way. The group moves through backstreets and side alleys, taking detours to avoid patrols. No alarm has been raised yet; the operation proceeds smoothly. The dilapidated school looms into view — a repurposed building surrounded by a chain-link fence. Two guards flank the front entrance. Others roam the perimeter.
Kurisu spots an opportunity: the buildings on the back side are uninhabited. A blind spot. Kent agrees — breach the fence, find a window, work fast. No deviations.
Pez is gone. No one saw him leave.
An explosion rocks the night from the back of the school.

Summary
The group charges toward the site of the explosion. Kent and Kurisu take the longer route, trying to reach Pez. Two Death’s Head patrol guards spot them and move to intercept.
Pug and Dust break off — a direct route. Pug runs up behind one guard, grabs his shoulder, and drives the combat knife into the back of his neck — splitting the vertebrae. Dust lunges at the other, their bandaged hands and feet transforming mid-air into jet-black talons. They claw into the guard’s throat and crash him to the ground, rolling forward without breaking stride.
Around the corner: Pez stands by the shrubbery, pointing at a hole blown in the school wall. “Hey! What’s up guys? Look! There’s an entrance.” Kent grabs him by the collar and charges through.
Inside, the hallway is dark. Two more guards round the far corner. Inmates appear from the left — a ragged group of six or more, eyes gleaming in the dim light.
Kent expands her armored bracer into a shield and draws an electrified baton. Pez raises a hand crossbow — the bolt flies between the charging inmates and embeds in a baseball bat. The fight is on.
Pug slides between Kent’s legs and slashes an inmate’s achilles tendon — the man drops to one knee. Kent’s electric baton crashes into his skull, pinning his head against the wall. Kent goads Pug on. Another inmate tackles Pug to the floor — Pug rolls on top and drives the knife into him over and over, relentless, until the man stops moving. Dust scales the walls with taloned hands and feet, dropping onto enemies from above — embedding claws into an inmate’s eyes, running up the wall, and crashing his head into the tile floor. Kurisu holds the rear against pursuing Death’s Head guards, using her case as a shield and a battering ram.
An inmate swings a baseball bat at Pug’s head — Pug sways back, the bat cracking into the wall beside him. Dust pounces from the ceiling, clamping onto his shoulders and raking his face. Pug kicks his own knife into another inmate’s forehead — the blade lodges deep. The man reaches for his face in shock as Pez’s bolt hits his shoulder, sending him down.
The fight ends. Inmates and guards lie still or groaning on the floor. Kurisu drives her case into the chin of the last armored biker.
“Alright! We don’t have much time. Move!” Kent charges forward. The group rounds the corner, deeper into the school.

Summary
The group exits the school into the dark streets. Time is around 9-10 PM. The buildings ahead glow dimly, illuminating the approaching Death’s Head — three dozen men, all hurrying toward the prison. The way back is cut off.
Pez states: “That’s not good.”
Kurisu scans the area — all the alleyways between the unused buildings have been blocked off by sheet metal walls bolted to the surrounding structures. There is no other path. One of the Abyss Hunters suggests the residential buildings. Pez shakes his head — breaking into residential buildings after nightfall violates a taboo of the Head. No one breaks the Head’s laws.
All doors are locked or reinforced from inside. Windows are intact or barred. Dust points at a nearby building with a drawing of a feather and a Z. Kent loses patience — “DUST! WORDS! PLEASE!” Dust writes: “not much left.”
Time runs short. The group tries alley after alley, finding them sealed with sheet metal bolted into the surrounding buildings. Finally, they find one where the sheet metal is broken — debris and collapsed furniture block part of it, but there is a gap large enough for a child to slip through. Dust cocks their head, nods vigorously, and squeezes through. A muffled explosion follows.
Kent watches with frustration. “Goddamnit. Dust always does whatever the Hell they want.”
The Death’s Head draw nearer. Kent offers Burr and Pug an escape: “If you two shitheads see an opening while we’re fighting, take it and get out of here.” Burr refuses. Kent is incredulous but relents. “We’re not staining the Office’s reputation.”
While the group braces, Pez shows Pug his ammunition — crossbow bolts tipped with runeclay, a tan clay-like substance. Pez portions out a small sphere of runeclay. “Sure! Just pay me back after.” Pug cuts a piece of his shirt to make a pouch for it, wrapping the runeclay inside. He lights the fabric on fire. Pez begins assembling a larger explosive charge.
Kent readies her shield and baton. “They’re almost here!”
Pez fires a bolt into the approaching Death’s Head, striking one in the chest. The first wave crashes upon them.

Summary
The Death’s Head wave crashes into the group. Kent blocks several with her shield, caving in a skull with her electrified baton. Pez fires bolts from the back line. Kurisu holds her case horizontally like a wall, the press of bodies pushing her backward, strikes landing on her shoulders and back.
One man charges at Pug. Pug sidesteps the swipe and drives the combat knife into his neck — the man gurgles and falls past him. A pipe strikes Pug’s arm. A boot catches him in the stomach. He stumbles back.
Burr blocks a lead pipe blow aimed at his side — it catches his arm instead. He drives an uppercut into the man’s solar plexus with his brass knuckles. Something collapses beneath the skin. The man falls backward as more push past him. Burr turns and punches another in the temple — the man drops instantly.
The Death’s Head begin to encircle the group. Kurisu slides backward under the weight of the press. Kent falls back behind her.
Pug trips a man trying to advance between them — the man falls, and Pug curbstomps the back of his neck. A sharp crunch. Another charges and tackles Pug — he braces, holds his ground, and plunges the combat knife into the man’s head. He shoves the body into the advancing line to trip another.
Pez calls out. “Okay! It’s done!” He throws a round object into the crowd. A moment passes — nothing. “Oh. That’s not good. I set it for 01 seconds.” Exactly ten seconds later, a massive shockwave erupts — like a grenade without fire or shrapnel, a deep bass reverb. Bodies and equipment fly in every direction.
Kent is thrown onto their back. Kurisu is pushed backward into Pez. Pug and Burr are thrown — Pug breaks his fall cleanly; Burr stumbles heavily but stays upright with his shield.
Pug, Pez, and Kurisu — carrying Kent — run through the field of downed enemies, firing nails and bolts at the fallen. Burr runs the opposite direction, back toward the ski-mask man. He hoists the wounded man in a fireman carry.
The remaining Death’s Head form a barricade, separating Burr from the others. More reinforcements approach from the station. Pug draws his handgun — two shots ring out. One Death’s Head falls.

An explosion tears through an alleyway blockade — debris flies, smoke and dust billowing. Two silhouettes emerge. A smaller figure in a black collared shirt with an undone tie, an open suit jacket, a cigarette in his mouth, an odd sword sheathed in his hand. Beside him, a massive figure — tank top over a heavily muscled body, tanned skin, a cocky expression, pocket chains and rings, and swirling tattoos that Burr recognizes immediately.
The Stray Dog Packleader.
Burr spins the ski-mask man around and heaves him over the Death’s Head barricade toward the others.
The man in the suit takes a puff. He proposes a deal: the Stray Dog “takes responsibility” for the mess. If he loses, they all walk.
Kent gives Pug and Burr paracord bracelets with painted beads — absorptive charms. She tightens them.
The fight is brutal. Burr meets the Stray Dog head-on — the knife cuts his armpit, drawing first blood. The Stray Dog’s knee catches Burr’s shield — the plexiglass shatters, Burr skidding several meters. Pug charges from behind — the reinforced cargo pants stop the knife. Pug reaches for his gun. The Stray Dog’s Special Move Punch catches Pug’s arm — he flies back, left forearm fractured. The bracelets’ beads shatter.
Kent is kicked, gets back up. Pez fires an explosive bolt — caught inches from the Stray Dog’s face. It detonates, staggering him. Kurisu swings her case into his side. Pug slashes his calf. Kent kicks his legs out, forcing him to kneel. Burr stabs for his throat — meets a metal suppression cuff. Pug slides and fires the handgun into his eye — the eye splits but does not penetrate. The metal cuffs break off.
The Stray Dog’s suppression is removed. He grins. Tattoos glow. He spins — shockwave. Kent crumples, coughing blood. Kurisu slides back. Pug is thrown, right arm aching. Burr is thrown, ribs cracking. The bracelets’ remaining power holds, then the beads snap.
The Stray Dog laughs, then looks at Kent. Kurisu kneels over her. Kent is dead.
John steps forward. He tosses a key to Kurisu. She unlocks her case — an anti-material rifle. “Evildoers will be punished.” Her eyes go unfocused.
The Stray Dog charges. Kurisu kicks off his fist, launches backward, and fires — a small hole enters his shoulder, then detonates from within. His arm separates. He keeps going. She drops the rifle, draws a shotgun — blasting a hole through his stomach. He grabs the shotgun, she swings under his legs, retrieves her case, and rains fire from dual pistols. The Stray Dog crumples. Falls.
John negotiates with the swordsman. The group is free to go.
The ski-mask man thanks Burr and departs.
Back at Diluc’s Tavern. John pays Pug — 75,000 for the contract. Change is returned. Pug pays 10,000 for a room with two twin beds.
Both agents sleep. Thirty minutes later, a muffled explosion from Dust’s room. Burr investigates — finds a smoking Pez behind her. Dust gives him a disappointed look, writes “dust” on her tablet, and closes the door.

Day 06 Summary

District 12, Post-Collapse — In-World Day 6
Agents: Pug (Welfare Department), Burr (Disciplinary Department)
The longest day of the campaign. Agents cross into Brotherhood territory, raid the Founder’s apartment, fight a cyborg, Burr bargains with his life, enters the Pound prison, massacres inmates, escapes with a cloaked ally, reunites with Pug and hired Fixers, and fights a Stray Dog packleader.

Key Events

5 AM wake-up at Koller’s workshop. Agents depart The Time Machine.
Morning fight with Death’s Head patrol near the clinic. Burr recognizes the father of a man he killed. All three subdued alive.
Checkpoint massacre discovered — the axe-man’s work. Burr finds Death’s Head gear in a dumpster. Puts it on.
Raid the cafe kitchen. Food obtained. Cafe investigated for the scent on the helmet.
Return to the Community. Death’s Head gear confiscated briefly, then retrieved. Bread knife and other knives retrieved from locker.
Meeting with Ben. Pug gives bread. Burr gives half-eaten tin of oats. Ben provides locations for the workshop key.
Retrieve gear from armory. Borrow baseball bat (Burr) and PVC pipe spear with knife (Pug) for impeding authorities.
Scavenger market encounter. Warehouse district. Death’s Head cookout sighted.
Augmented checkpoint fight. Burr kills two. Harness augments fail.
Enter Brotherhood territory. Find the Founder’s apartment. Extensive looting — bayonet, keys, tools, cash, sealed containers, pills.
Cyborg fight in an alley. Burr acquires a damaged chainsaw sword. Pug burns his palm.
Burr captured at a reinforced Death’s Head checkpoint after fighting Brick (sergeant-at-arms).
Pug escapes through alleys, enters a pawn shop. Meets Kurisu (Grade 6 Fixer, Abyss Hunter Office).
Pawn shop fight. Kurisu defeats Death’s Head thugs. Pug sustains upper arm bruise.
Pug meets the Abyss Hunter Office: Pez, Dust, and Kent. Contract signed for 75,000.
Burr interrogated by a tired Death’s Head interrogator. Bargains his life with Stray Dog intel. Sent to the Pound (abandoned school prison).
Burr massacres the Pound: kills two inmates at the entrance, four in a classroom, meets the eyepatch man (blonde, one eye, searching for his compound bow), meets the ski-mask man (black tank top, one-hole mask), kills two thugs alongside him, fights through the broadcasting room against the Pound Boss. Acquires cloak, nailgun, and shield from a storage closet.
Pug and the Abyss Hunters infiltrate the Pound. Explosion at the back wall. Fight through the school entrance hall — Pug kills a guard and two inmates. Dust reveals claw augmentations.
Reunion — Pug and Burr find each other inside the school. Burr hands the nailgun to Pug. Ski-mask man is patched up.
The group exits the school to find three dozen Death’s Head blocking the way. The back alleys are sealed with sheet metal.
Pez explains the Head’s taboo — residential buildings cannot be breached at night. Dust squeezes through a gap.
The Death’s Head wave hits. Pug kills three, Burr kills two. Pez throws an explosive charge — shockwave scatters the enemy.
The Stray Dogs arrive. A swordsman in a suit and the tattooed Stray Dog Packleader. The swordsman negotiates a duel.
Final battle. Kent gives Burr and Pug protective bracelets. The fight is brutal — Pug’s forearm is fractured, his shield is destroyed. Kent is killed. Kurisu unleashes her case’s contents: an anti-material rifle, shotgun, and dual pistols. The Stray Dog’s arm is blown off. He falls.
The group is freed. The ski-mask man thanks Burr and departs.
Return to Diluc’s Tavern. Payment of 75,000 made. Change returned. 10,000 paid for a room.
Night. A muffled explosion from Pez’s room. Burr investigates. Dust — revealed as a small, pale girl — answers the door, a smoking Pez behind her. She accepts a headpat and closes the door.

The night passes. The Sweepers rumble through the streets. Both agents wake early, gripped by heavy stomach cramps and parched throats. Their bodies, no longer sustained by adrenaline, complain heavily from the abuse of the past day.
They crawl downstairs. The bartender greets them with a nod. Breakfast is 1,000 per plate, each with orange-flavored water. They buy two plates. Pez and Dust come down. Summary
The agents reach the Time Machine. Pug reflects on Koller’s directions and begins navigating. The Death’s Head territory is uneventful — unfamiliar streets with the same gang symbols. The patrols are sparse, tired, and many are visibly injured.
A black cat darts into the street and stops in the middle of the road. It is thin, matted, and emaciated. It watches them warily. Burr tears open one of the travel ration pouches. Inside: a greyish-brown, thick, slightly clumpy liquid. He finds a small tin can and pours the contents in — the liquid sludges out slowly. The smell is an odd mixture of cooked mushrooms and canned tuna.
He sets the can down and steps back. The cat sniffs the air, locks onto the can, and slowly approaches. It snatches the can, carries it a few meters away, and laps up the liquid. After finishing, it approaches Pug cautiously, sniffs his hand, and allows him to scratch under its chin. It begins to follow them.
Rapid footsteps from an alleyway. A young man skids to a halt, gasping for breath. He is in a grey hooded jacket with a small sword sheathed at his hip — a lower-quality blade with visible weld marks. “You! You two! T-That cat… Could you help me catch it? I’m trying to get it back to its owners.”
He shows a Fixer card. Finn, Grade 9 Fixer of Grade 8 Yun’s Office. Pug picks up the cat and hands it to him. Finn is overjoyed. He scrambles for his wallet and hands Pug 8,500 Ahn — apologizing that he hasn’t been paid yet for his current job. He insists he cannot accept more than his job’s pay of 10,000 as a reward.
Finn explains the sword is a gift from his sister, who used her savings to buy it from a workshop. He promised to become a successful Fixer. He takes the cat with great care and heads back into the alleyway.
The agents continue onward. A Death’s Head checkpoint ahead — barely more than a broken couch and debris with a single man on a folding chair. He waves them through without a word. They leave the Death’s Head territory behind and venture into the uncontrolled areas.

Summary
The streets narrow. The buildings pack closer together, their height shrinking to one or two stories topped with sheet metal shanty roofs. The atmosphere is winding and claustrophobic.
They pass a man walking in the same direction — a small school backpack too small for him, a thick jacket, a beanie, and a crowbar in his hands. He glances at them as they pass, watching without hostility.
Following the road, they reach an area of destroyed buildings. Collapsed concrete walls with rusty bent rebar. Shards of glass and debris scatter across the narrow streets. The sky is clearer without intact buildings blocking it. Cracks run through the ground — a fissure splits the street, as if from an earthquake.
They hop over the fissure and continue. A large debris barrier blocks the path — collapsed walls and metal roof tiling forming a small, scalable wall. Burr climbs over without hesitation, instinctively placing his feet and trusting his holds. Pug follows more carefully, testing each handhold before committing. Both make it over without incident.
The ground on the other side is higher, sloping toward a center point. They descend into the ruins, surrounded by buildings too destroyed to house anything — collapsed from whatever caused the earth to cave in at the center.

Summary
Inside the ruins, a staircase descends into complete darkness. The agents hold the railing, navigating by touch through the pitch-black corridor. Pug retrieves and switches on the flashlight.
Pug yanks the first door open. A string snaps — a metal can falls from above and clatters across the floor. A simple alarm trap. Nothing follows.
The first floor is a large looted office space: toppled cubicles, tipped water dispensers, emptied of anything valuable.
The second floor has a fire burning inside — warm air gusting out. Burr drops low and creeps toward the light. Two dead bodies: one on the floor, one slumped at a desk. Behind the body on the floor, under the desk, a small drawstring backpack sits. Burr retrieves it. Contents: a small tin of food, several staplers, a coffee mug, and a mostly used office tape dispenser. He leaves the water bottle behind as too risky.
A sound behind them near the fire. They withdraw and head to the third floor.

Summary
The third floor is dark and identical to the first — cleared office space, no traps, nothing of value.
The fourth floor is different. The door’s window is shattered, and a large table has been pushed against it from the inside. Pug reaches through the broken window and shoves the table repeatedly until it slides far enough to allow a crack. The door catches on something — a body, they discover later — but a small opening is created.
Burr peers through the crack. He sees desks that have NOT been cleared out like the floors above — and several figures on the floor, unmoving.
They force the door open. The table topples over a desiccated corpse in a charcoal grey suit. The room is filled with withered, shriveled bodies — all wearing the same uniform: a charcoal grey two-button suit with a matching red tie. Badges bear an insignia: an “L” like a railroad spike being driven into a brain from below. Many died from blunt force trauma, office supplies still clutched in their death grips.
A janitor’s closet holds horrors best left undescribed: desiccated bodies missing limbs, clothing stripped, broken scissors and a broken paper-cutting blade nearby.
The manager’s office holds a hanging body — a suicide from the broken ceiling fan. Pug takes down the body and coils the rope into the drawstring bag. On the desk: a folded letter and a letter opener. The letter details the building’s entombment — a company intercom message, an alarm, concrete replacing the windows. Survivors fled to lower floors, raided for supplies. The floor manager locked the door and the key in the safe, dooming them all. The author chose suicide over starvation.
A small office safe sits in the corner. Footsteps echo from the staircase above — the other groups are arriving.

Summary
The agents descend further. The air grows humid and warm. The grey walls darken with a reddish tint. A heartbeat begins to thrum in the back of their minds — slow, rhythmic. Thump thump. Thump thump.
Burr’s foot lands on something soft. Pink flesh covers the stairs, spreading down the walls. Blueish veins and dark red arteries run across the surfaces like cables. The flesh grows thicker as they descend.
At the bottom floor, there is no door. Instead, a fleshy valve pulses open and closed in time with the heartbeat. Burr times it and hops through. Pug hesitates — then jumps. The valve closes on the back of his duster before opening again, releasing him.
Two hallways branch ahead: straight, leading to three rooms and restrooms; and right, with a power symbol visible far down. They take the right path. The humid, claustrophobic air presses in around them.
Four sets of elevators stand in the middle of the corridor. In the center, a figure in a charcoal grey suit stands utterly still, gazing at the floor. A mop handle is held in its hand like a staff. Every few seconds, a tremor passes through its body in sync with the heartbeat.
Burr steps forward, avoiding the fleshy patches on the floor. The figure’s head snaps up, its back arching slightly as it gazes at the ceiling. The heartbeat accelerates. Burr steps carefully, keeping to the thinnest membrane where possible.
At three meters, a particularly heavy thump reverberates through their skulls. The figure turns.
A short-haired man. His clothes are covered in fleshy membrane that connects to his own skin. Veins spread across his cheek, pouring into an eye socket. His remaining eye is dull and unfocused.
For Burr, a stirring from within — anxious, but also something else. Recognition of a threat.
For Pug, a wave of wrongness. This thing before them is inhuman.
The figure’s face stops inches from Pug’s. The heartbeat becomes a rapid drumming. A bloodcurdling screech echoes within their minds.

Burr hurled a chunk of broken wall at it, striking the flesh mass. The creature did not react. Pug shook up a can of the Unknown chemical and threw it. The can struck the creature’s arms with a dull squelch and dropped to the floor. Something shifted in the creature: its heart swelled, beating faster, red swirls joining the blue.
The agents scrambled for the elevators. Three were closed and powerless. The fourth had its doors cracked open, the elevator floor a step below the hallway. Pug squeezed through first. Burr’s helmet caught between the doors. He threw the helmet at the creature and slipped inside.
Pug pushed Burr up through the elevator hatch. As Pug turned to pull Burr up, the creature’s arms swung forward. It released an intense psychic scream and shockwave. Both agents were knocked down, Pug onto the elevator roof, Burr to the floor. The creature began hammering the elevator doors, denting them inward with increasing speed.
Pug pulled Burr onto the roof. They jumped, trying to move the elevator. No ladder, no lever, no way down. Burr stabbed at the braking system with a knife. The material would not budge, only blunting the blade.
The creature’s strikes accelerated, the doors bending, beginning to break. Then its heart began to thump erratically, turning gray and still. The creature stopped mid-punch, arms dropping, flesh retreating. The building’s thumping returned to its initial slow rhythm.
Burr dropped down cautiously. The creature still moved with the building’s rhythm but did not react to approach. He searched its pockets and found a single key. With the key and flashlight, he headed north to the Janitor’s Office, unlocked it, and the two agents entered. Inside: empty cleaning solution bottles, janitorial supplies, and a latchbox on the wall. Rows upon rows of keys inside. They grabbed all the keys, stuffed them in their pockets, and headed to the power room. After trying between twenty and thirty keys, the door clicked open. Breaker boxes and switches lined the walls. The lights flickered on. Alarms began blaring.

The creature has recovered from earlier and is back in combat stance. Burr tries an elevator — it opens. Inside, an unmarked button at the bottom opens to reveal a keyhole when pressed. Burr begins trying keys from the keyring. None fit.
The creature’s heartbeat swells. A psychic shockwave blasts both agents against the elevator walls. The creature begins thumping against the elevator doors. Summary
Down the hall, led by one of the turtleneck man’s colleagues, a large entourage filters into the reception area. Far more people than before: a mixture of scavengers and more seasoned individuals, many carrying backpacks and equipment on belts and straps. At least one of the fixer-looking individuals from earlier is among them. The group spreads out, some sitting, most standing. The more opportunistic-looking scavengers seem out of their element. The tension is palpable; many avoid the walls.
A tall, lanky man steps up behind the reception desk, using it like a podium. He wears a boonie hat with a neck covering, a grey poncho over a fancy brown suit, a monocle, a pocket chain, and a well-groomed handlebar mustache. A satchel hangs at his left side. He carries a small brass-colored staff like a walking cane, holding it more like a king’s scepter.
He calls Pug and Burr forward. He scrutinizes them, adjusts his monocle, and commends them for their scouting contributions. He notes their ambition for the group to observe and learn from. The tension in the room thickens as stares bore into the agents’ backs.
He introduces himself as Sir Tatum the Third. He produces a small leatherbound notebook and feather pen, scribbling notes. When Burr presents a key from the creature, Sir Tatum adds it to his list of contributions.
He unfurls a contract: a temporary employment agreement under Sir Tatum III, with pay determined by contributions. The contract is approved and upheld by the Oufi South Section 5. The agents sign. Sir Tatum welcomes them and declares the expedition will proceed immediately.
Burr transfers one elevator key to the turtleneck man to aid the expedition.

Burr’s group: Sir Tatum III, Fixer 2, the turtleneck man’s bandana-wearing colleague, the raincoat individual, two scavengers, and two explorers.
Burr’s elevator descends first by a few seconds. Sir Tatum is giddy, nearly bouncing with excitement. “Ahaaa! What fun! I can hardly hold my excitement.” He reminds the group that if he dies, nobody gets paid. The ride is long, several minutes of steady descent. Summary
The elevators open onto an underground facility. Yellow-tinted metal paneling forms the walls, coated in flesh that pulses visibly with the heartbeat. Metal pipes run across the walls and ceiling. Soft fluorescent light glows overhead. Something about this place feels deeply familiar.
Both groups filter into the landing room. Sir Tatum III peers around with starry eyes, taking a deep breath of the stale, musky air. “Gentlemen! This is it. We stand upon the shoulders of giants. This here… is one of the ruined branches of the Fallen Wing.”
He warns the assembled group of rumors of monsters akin to those in the Outskirts. Most of the party reacts with fear, shock, and disgust. One scavenger doubles over and vomits. Many seem to see the flesh clearly for the first time. “This isn’t mold,” one Fixer mutters.
Two hallways branch from the room: left and right, both identical. Tatum calls for everyone to gather and issues instructions: secure any green liquid found, report anything unnatural without engaging. He takes a seat at a small cafeteria table. “Good luck, my brave adventurers. I look forward to your good results.”
Pug heads left with the turtleneck man, his two colleagues, and two scavengers. The explorers and Fixers wait in the room for reinforcements. The raincoat individual heads right. Burr separates from the group during the movement.

Summary
Burr changes the channel. A black and white video plays — handheld footage of two children playing on a playground beneath heavy smog. The children stop and gaze at a point in the distance, one gesturing for the cameraman to look. The camera is dropped, facing trees as the smog-filled sky illuminates. The trees shake. The video cuts back to the start.
Through bearing witness, it will not be forgotten. That day was not one to forget. Burr raises his hand to change the channel again — to live through the day once more, to continue to bear witness.
He forces himself to switch back to static. He sits before the static television, wondering why a sealed room holds a television that plays nothing. He changes the channel once more and finds himself in a park, holding a camera. His children play on the playground before him. It is not often he gets time off to spend with them. Something is deeply wrong.
He drops the camera and runs to grab his children. Something is deeply wrong — he needs to get out. He hugs them both. One asks what is wrong. Smoke blankets the horizon. Something white shoots into the sky, piercing the smog. A pillar of light tears into the heavens. The cityscape and treelines are bathed in light. The trees sway as the breeze picks up.
He tells them nothing is wrong, but tears pour from his eyes. His children cry, wordlessly entranced by the light. He finds himself unable to look away either. The uncertainty melts away. He realizes why there are tears — it reminds him of a beautiful sunrise from his youth, when he was still hopeful about the future, before the smog covered the skies. The light is simply beautiful.
He picks his children up onto his shoulders and finds himself staring at a fluorescent bulb. The television has returned to static. He ponders what he has been doing. A warm feeling lingers in his chest. He pats the television and heads toward the door, which slides open for him.
Changes

Summary
The door slides shut behind Burr. He feels something pressed against his face. A pair of old-style glasses frames, no lenses, resting on the bridge of his nose. Their presence fills him with warmth he cannot explain.
A slot in the wall rumbles. Something clunks down a pipe and strikes the compartment below, sounding like a vending machine dispensing its contents. He retrieves a yellow and red canister, half-filled with a glowing, bubbling light-green liquid. The smell shifts as he inhales. Earth, then paint, then freshly cut grass, cycling endlessly. The throb in his broken wrist eases. His body begins to relax.
He takes a sip. It tastes like seltzer water. Warmth spreads from his mouth down his throat, radiating through his body. His aches and pains fade to a whisper, though the wounds themselves remain. His head grows heavy. His body sluggish. A profound sense of peace settles over him, the feeling that everything will be alright.
He chugs the rest.
His body turns to lead. The warmth becomes an unbearable burn, as though he were staring directly into the sun. He falls forward, vomiting green liquid across the floor. The pain vanishes. So does the feeling of his body. He blacks out.

Pug heads down the left hallway with the three dark-clothed individuals (turtleneck man, ski mask, bandana) and two scavengers following close behind. The hall splits — the left branch is overtaken by a larger fleshmass that covers the lights and walls, sealing hermetically sealed metal doors beneath its bulk. At the end of the hall, something pulses and glows within one of the larger growths on the wall. Three bodies lie on the floor before it, faintly illuminated.
The man in the turtleneck warns it smells like a trap. One scavenger pushes forward anyway, declaring “Pussyshit. Can’t let you hog all the glory.” He loots the bodies — finds nothing worth selling, the flesh having ruined everything. He tugs a jacket from the second body, then stops. He turns toward the glowing fleshmass. “Oi… Any of you lot back there.. hear some beating?”
He walks toward it. “It’s my heart… My heart’s in there! It’s MINE!” His arms sink into the flesh. A pulse of light flashes, then darkness. When the light returns, the scavenger stands with his torso torn open — a pulsing, light red glow within his chest. “I’ve done it lads! I’m feelin’ the best I’ve EVER felt before!” He is transformed, aggressive, triumphant.
Pug cuts away flesh from one containment unit window. Inside: a bedroom — blue walls, comic books on the floor, clothes scattered. The ski mask man helps cut at another window, but the flesh regrows too fast. The group moves on, no one having a flamethrower.

Summary
Pug examines the two vending machines against the wall. The left is black and gray — empty, formerly containing snacks. The right is purple and orange, featuring a cartoon shrimp giving a thumbs up while holding an open can of purple soda.
There is no way to open either machine. One button for product, a slot for bills, a dispensing hole at the bottom, but no change return. Pug presses the button — the machine lights up like a retro arcade. The bill slot glows with an outline.
Pug inserts his own ID badge. The display reads: INSUFFICIENT BALANCE. It ejects. He inserts 100 Ahn. Still insufficient. Another 400 Ahn — a total of 500 — and a can clunks down. It is purple with the shrimp mascot. Grape flavor.
Pug takes a sip — sweet, refreshing, cool. He chugs half. Green sparkles shed from his skin. His fractured left forearm stops hurting — the fracture is healed.
The turtleneck man returns from the locker room with several IDs. One reads: “Martin, Control Team Agent II.” Pug slots Martin’s card into the machine — another can dispenses. Pug’s purple can powderizes into sand as the new one drops. This one is light blue — lime flavored, sprite-like. Pug pockets it.
He notices six cameras around the room: one at each hallway entrance, one above each armory door, one facing the blank wall, and one in the center ceiling. Approaching the blank wall opposite the armory doors, he finds a small panel — not quite flush. It clicks open. Inside: a horizontal slot identical to the vending machine’s, and a small black screen angled out. Pug slots Martin’s card. A fingerprint prompt appears on the screen. Pug’s thumb — scanned. The screen flashes green. A panel opens, revealing a set of elevator doors.
Behind him, Burr falls to the floor — just barely regaining consciousness.

Summary
Burr stumbles forward, using the table for support. His legs barely work — he feels the cold tile floor on his bare feet. Pug stands at the vending machine, watching his friend crawl back from the brink of death.
The room watches quietly as Pug uses Martin’s card. A red soda clatters down. Burr chugs it — green sparkles shed from his skin. Many of his minor injuries heal completely. His forearm aches less, though his wrist still does not work. His head still swims — a massive hangover from the overdose.
Another soda dispenses — light blue, lime-flavored. Burr chugs it. The remaining nausea, vertigo, and thrumming in his head subside. His mouth feels dry — the soda has left him dehydrated, but the overdose effects are gone.
Pug confronts the scavengers about Burr’s pants and boots. They return the gear for 3,000 Ahn compensation. A quiet scavenger offers a half-drunk water bottle for 500. Pug buys it. The water is stale with grit and sediment, but the dehydration fades slightly.
Burr takes the lensless spectacles off his face and puts them on Pug. They vanish. Burr feels them — they are back on his face. The raincoat individual watches silently.
The group gathers at the hidden elevator. The turtleneck man salutes — his group will stay behind to try opening the armory. Everyone else crams into the elevator: Pug, Burr, the raincoat individual, the transformed scavenger (whose heart still thumps audibly in the enclosed space), and the other scavengers. Two buttons inside. The doors close. They descend.

While Pug works the monitors, Burr’s hallway door slides open. He approaches a dark room and hears rapid, shallow breathing within his mind. The breathing grows louder as he nears. He finds a white padded room. Peeking inside, chains rattle, and the breathing stops. A raspy telepathic voice pleads, speaking of its neck hurting, of everyone watching, of the lever dropping, of being forgotten. It begs to be killed. Burr steps inside; the door slides shut behind him. The hallway light flickers on — an old lantern casting a soft glow. A seven-foot figure sits on the ground, wrists and neck bound by a broken stockade, head covered in a burlap sack with dark stains at the eyes, a noose tying the sack to the neck. Broken shackles and chains hang from its wrists. The entity, the Forgotten Murderer, begs increasingly manically for death — to be hanged, choked, cut open. Burr refuses. He approaches and removes the burlap sack and cuts the noose. The stockade and manacles clatter to the floor. The Forgotten Murderer vanishes, nowhere to be found.
Burr grabs a saw and axe from the room, but they turn to mist as he steps outside. The door closes, and chains rattle within. A dispenser to the side of the door dispenses a half-full canister of green liquid, then a suit: a yellowed collared shirt, brown suit with burlap reinforcements, noose tie, chained cuffs, burlap half-mask, and a tallied belt with hammerspace pockets. He dons the suit over his existing clothes — his cloak, nailgun, helmet, vest, pants, boots, armband, and lanyard remain hidden beneath the magical garment. The suit shifts his visible appearance entirely, replacing his silhouette with that of the Forgotten Murderer, but all his original gear is still there, concealed beneath the burlap-reinforced fabric. He slides the canister into the suit’s hammerspace pocket, where it disappears until mentally retrieved. Burr returns to Pug.

Cherry blossom petals blink into existence above and drift slowly downward through the warm air. At the far end of the room, on a simple wooden stand, sits a suit of ruined samurai armor. Dented, tarnished, aged and worn. Three murals in traditional ink style adorn the surrounding walls. Armored leaders clashing on a battlefield. A black-armored samurai kneeling, headless, in ritual death. A lone man in a simple tunic standing against an overwhelming force, his horse bristling with embedded weapons.
Pug approaches the armor. Piece by piece he lifts it from the stand and begins to don it. The greaves, the cuirass, the shoulder guards, the helmet. As each piece settles onto his body, ancient rust and tarnish flake away, revealing gleaming pristine steel beneath. A voice speaks into his mind, telepathic, ancient, patient. The spirit within the armor promises invincibility to a worthy ruler who can bring order to chaos. The armor gleams with renewed purpose, every dent and scratch erased, as though forged anew.

Summary
Pug and Burr continue down the hall. Around the corner, another hallway gives way to a set of stairs descending into darkness. A layer of black smoke obscures everything below.
Pug’s eyes sting and water as they descend, the acrid mist burning. For Burr, the air feels suffocating. His suit constricts too tightly, the rope around his neck tightening. Not enough to choke, but enough to keep him acutely aware of it, forcing him to focus on each breath. Burr tells it to show itself. Nothing happens. A slow, rhythmic wood creaking echoes from below, like something large swaying back and forth. Pug slips on the stairs. Burr catches him before he falls.
At the bottom, the black fog is thicker, pooling along the floor. An open containment unit on one wall pours miasma into the corridor, and from within comes the same slow creaking, louder now, resonant. The room inside is drained of all color, as though the fog has leeched every hue from it. Old splintered walls. A floor caked in decades of dust. The door clicks shut behind them, sealing them in.
A lighthouse-like beam of light sweeps slowly across the room, casting long shadows through the haze. A voice speaks, not aloud, but within their minds. The Old Man’s internal monologue filters through. Apathetic, weary, questioning. He does not address them directly. He is lost in his own thoughts, talking to himself.
Pug moves forward alone. Ahead, the Old Man sits, massive in stature but impossibly frail, dressed in a black suit and hat, hunched over a cane. His back is turned, his attention fixed on a painting. It depicts a Christmas Eve scene. A wagon piled high with gifts in a snow-covered landscape. The horses have run off. Someone has walked miles through the bitter cold, hauling the wagon alone.
As Pug watches, the painting shimmers and strains at the edges, as though the canvas can barely contain what is painted on it. The dark corners of the room press inward. Burr reaches out and touches the painting, and disappears, pulled into the canvas. Pug touches it as well, and vanishes too.

Summary
Pug and Burr stand in a snowy forest. A narrow path stretches ahead, vanishing into an endless white horizon. Snow falls steadily from a grey sky, blanketing the ground and the trees in silence. There is no wind. No rustling of leaves. Only the persistent, gentle fall of snow.
A voice speaks from behind them. An older man stands there, weathered and tired, wearing a grey suit spattered with blood and a fedora. The broken haft of an arrow protrudes from one of his legs. Several more jut from his back. Patches of his suit are blackened with soot and burn marks. He carries a large, bulging sack.
“Just an old man trying to make it home,” he says.
He limps forward through the snow, leaving a trail of blood behind him. Burr offers to carry the sack. The moment he takes the weight, it drops to the ground as though made of lead. Burr strains, but cannot lift it, not even an inch. The old man watches. Then, with one hand, he picks it up again, effortlessly, as though it weighs nothing.
“You’ve tried. That’s enough,” he says.
He limps onward. He mentions that it is Christmas Eve and invites them to stay. In the distance, through the snow, the warm glow of lights flickers. A house with a chimney, smoke rising against the grey sky.
Pug and Burr look closer at the world around them. The trees, the snow, the old man himself. Everything seems wrong. Smudged, blurred at the edges, as though it has been painted. The snow has no texture. The old man’s wounds look like brushstrokes. Burr licks his thumb and wipes at one of the arrows in the old man’s back. It smudges. The arrow, the blood, the suit, all of it. Paint.
The old man looks at them, and then he is gone. They are back in the original room, standing in front of the painting on the wall. The canvas shows a snowy Christmas Eve scene. There is no blood on the floor. The old man is nowhere to be seen. The only sound is the faint creaking of the Old Man’s presence somewhere deeper in the room. But they both remember.

Summary
The painting comes off the wall with a heavy, resonant weight — as if the canvas itself is reluctant to leave its place. Pug holds it, the painted Christmas Eve scene frozen in snow and moonlight, the abandoned wagon and the long footprints stretching into the distance.
They find the Old Man in his room, still hunched and motionless, staring at the now-empty space where the painting hung. The black smoke pours from his back more heavily than before, coiling and writhing in the air like living things. When Pug touches him with the painting, nothing happens — no reaction, no recognition. The room is dead silent save for the slow creak of the Old Man’s breathing.
They search the room. Splotches of dried blood are scattered across the dull, grey walls — walls that look as if they have been scorched by an ancient fire, the color leeched from every surface. The room feels wrong, forgotten, steeped in decades of solitude and grief.
Burr takes the painting from Pug. In one decisive motion, he snaps it in half over his knee — the canvas tearing, the wooden frame cracking with a sharp report. The painted Christmas Eve scene splits, the snow-scape breaking into two jagged halves.
The Old Man’s head snaps up. A scream tears from his throat — raw, inhuman, a sound of pure anguish. “What have you done to my home?!” The walls tremble. The black smoke surges, thickening, churning. From the shadows behind the Old Man, something begins to stir — a tall, hunched figure unfolds itself, rising to twice the height of a man, its proportions wrong, its limbs too long. It wields a cane like a spear, the wood dark and polished, clutched in a skeletal grip.
The creature attacks.
Burr is caught in the first onslaught. The cane descends like a guillotine — a single strike that crushes Burr’s left arm completely, splattering flesh and bone across the floor. Before he can react, another strike catches his right shin, the bone snapping with a wet crack and protruding through the skin. A third blow fractures his left leg, the limb buckling beneath him. A sweeping strike pulverizes his right shoulder and arm, crushing them into pieces. The force of the blows sends blood spraying from Burr’s nose and ears. His vision swims. The world sounds distant, muffled — his hearing is already failing from the concussive trauma. He collapses, a broken heap on the grey floor.
Pug charges in. The samurai armor glimmers as he moves, putting himself between Burr and the creature. A wall of force slams into him — the creature’s power warping the room itself, debris and stone crashing against Pug’s armored frame. The samurai armor absorbs the impact, but one pauldron tears free and clatters to the ground, the ancient metal groaning in protest.
The cane whips toward Pug next. He raises his shinguard to block — the impact is catastrophic. The shinguard explodes into fragments, ceramic and steel shards scattering across the floor. The armor spirit screams in his mind, a telepathic howl of pain and fury.
Through ringing ears and blurred vision, Pug draws his E.G.O. handgun. He levels it at the Old Man’s face — at the weeping, ancient eye that stares through the chaos. He fires. Once. Twice. Three times.
Each round punches into the Old Man’s eye socket. The third shot drives deep. The Old Man recoils, a wet, guttural scream tearing from his throat as he stumbles back, clutching at his ruined eye. The hunched figure freezes, its cane faltering mid-swing.
The Old Man is stunned — temporarily blinded, disoriented by the shots to his eye. The black smoke wavers, thinning, losing its cohesive fury.
Pug grabs Burr by whatever remains of his collar and drags him toward the door. Burr is barely conscious, his limbs hanging at unnatural angles, blood pooling beneath him. Pug’s ears ring from the gunfire and the concussive blasts — a high-pitched whine drowning out all other sound, his hearing damaged by the violence of the encounter.
They escape the room, leaving the Old Man clutching his face, the hunched figure standing motionless over the shattered remains of the painting. The black smoke begins to swirl again, slow at first, then building — a promise that the respite will not last.

Pug drags Burr away from the Old Man’s chamber, pulling him across the floor and up the stairs. As they ascend, an arm reaches out of the containment unit, grasping toward them — a desperate, reaching motion from within the fog. The entire facility rumbles and shakes as “he” continues moving through it, a deep, resonant vibration felt through the walls and floor. Pug struggles to shut a door behind them, but it refuses to close properly, unable to seal the threshold.
Hurriedly, Pug pulls Burr up the staircase, his torso and legs thudding heavily against each step as he is dragged upward. Burr’s injuries are revealed in full: his right shoulder and everything below it is simply gone, a catastrophic wound leaving only torn flesh and exposed bone. His left arm is also missing entirely. A shard of bone protrudes from his shin, jagged and splintered through the skin. He is barely conscious, hanging limp as Pug hauls him step by step.
Reaching the top of the stairs, Pug peers down into the fog below. The raincoat individual dashes past, grabbing Burr’s legs to help carry the load. The raincoat yells and points toward the camera room — the direction of the elevator, the only escape route.
They reach the camera room. Inside, they find scavengers in the elevator. The elevator doors are closing. Its interior is splattered with blood, pooling and streaked across the walls and floor. One scavenger lies dead on the floor of the elevator, unmoving in a spreading stain. Another scavenger — the one who had given Pug water earlier — is seated inside, choking and coughing up blood. He grabs at Pug’s pant leg, desperately asking for help as the life drains from him.
The shaking continues. “He” is approaching. The raincoat individual presses the elevator button. The doors close.

Summary
The elevator ascends. Its interior is stained with blood — splotches and splatters across the walls and floor, cast back from the scavengers within. One scavenger lies dead on the floor, gunshot wounds in his stomach and shoulder. The other — the water-giver from earlier — is seated, alive but wounded, choking and coughing. Miasma hangs thick in the enclosed space, curling through the air.
The raincoat man ducks to the side, positioning himself out of the immediate line of fire from the opening doors. Burr hangs limp between Pug and the turtleneck man, barely conscious, his broken body suspended between the two.
The doors open onto the camera room. The turtleneck man — moving with urgency — approaches a vending machine against the far wall. He dispenses a light blue soda, its color pale and luminescent like a lime-flavored Sprite. He hands it to Pug.
Pug chugs it.
The effect is immediate. The tinnitus that had been screaming in his ears — the high-pitched whine from the Old Man’s concussive cane strikes and the gunfire — begins to fade. His hearing returns, muffled at first, then clearer. Blood stops dripping from his ears. His head still swims, his nose still bleeds, but the worst of the auditory damage is gone.
Seeing this, Pug turns to the vending machine. He dispenses a red soda — a deep crimson, glowing faintly. He brings it to Burr’s lips.
Burr drinks. The red liquid flows down his throat. He wakes — consciousness returning in a rush. Green sparkles dance across his body, a shimmering light that crawls over his wounds. He chugs the rest of the can. The green light intensifies, pulsing across torn flesh and mangled limbs.
Pug then dispenses a purple soda from the machine. He drinks. Blue and green sparkles erupt across his body — his right arm knits itself full and whole, the torn muscle and shattered bone restoring in seconds. His left leg follows, the fractures sealing, the flesh smoothing. His hearing returns fully. His vision, which had been blurred and swimming, snaps back into focus. Only his nose still bleeds.
The turtleneck man pays 500 Ahn for a second blue soda. He hands it to Pug. Pug chugs it. Blue sparkles cascade over him — his vision normalizes completely. His arm and leg are fully intact, the last traces of damage erased. His nose finally stops bleeding.
Pug is fully healed. Every injury from the Old Man’s assault — the hearing loss, the tinnitus, the blurred vision, the damage to his arm and leg — is gone.
Burr, meanwhile, drinks the purple soda Pug offers him. Blue and green sparkles wash over him. The bleeding from his ears stops. His hearing returns. He is less delirious, more present, able to track the world around him.
But the soda cannot do everything. His body is still a ruin. His left arm remains destroyed from the elbow down — a shattered mess of bone and torn flesh. The bone still protrudes from his right shin. Fingers are missing from his hands. A hole gapes in his cheek, the flesh punched through. Chunks of his body are simply gone, torn out by the Old Man’s assault. He is alive, awake, and thinking clearly — but far from whole.
The turtleneck man investigates the door leading out of the camera room. He applies thermite to the frame — the chemical burns white-hot, sputtering against the metal. When it cools, the door is untouched, marked only by cosmetic scorch marks, the mechanism still sealed. He tries Martin’s ID card against the reader. It does not work. The door refuses to open.
Of the four scavengers who descended into the Old Man’s floor, only two remain alive — the water-giver seated in the elevator, and the turtleneck man himself. Two are dead, their bodies left behind or lying in the elevator, their deaths occurring off-screen with no agent involvement.
Burr descends back to the Information Department alone, parting ways with Pug and the turtleneck man as they continue their investigation on this floor.

Summary
The group makes their way toward the armory. While Pug and the others approach the armory doors, Burr searches the adjacent camera room. The air is thick with miasma — both in the hallway outside and within the computer room itself. Taking a deep breath, Burr enters and begins cycling through the camera feeds.
Switching to the Control Department cameras, Burr flicks through them. The feeds show containment units — most are dark and unremarkable. One catches his eye. He stops for a moment. The image is mostly dark, but there is a body hanging upside down from the ceiling — one of the scavengers from earlier.
Burr approaches the armory door and swipes his ID badge. The display reads: MATCHING ID NOT FOUND. A moment passes. Then, the door clicks open — it works. The armory lies ahead.
Inside the armory, four lockers are discovered, each containing distinct items:
Locker 1 — A brown fuzzy two-piece suit, resembling a child’s toy. Equipped with kneepads and elbow pads, stuffed hemming, brown gloves, and a ragged bowtie.
Locker 2 — A long weapon: a cross or mace with a skull at its head, bound in red thorns. It appears inanimate — until Burr cuts his finger and lets blood drip onto the skull. The blood activates it.
Locker 3 (The Old Man’s) — A dark funeral suit: a two-piece suit in choking black, a white shirt with a light stain, pointed shoes, black leather gloves, and a faint black miasma emanating from it. A lever-action rifle — brown wood stock, shifting gunmetal, dark miasma drifting from the barrel. A small cane topped with a black fedora.
Locker 4 — A long Victorian detective coat, a white shirt with a brown tie and pendant, brown pinstripe pants, and leather gloves. A shattered glass knife — its pattern shifting and changing as it catches the light.
As items are claimed, contention arises over the glass knife. Pug and the raincoat individual both reach for it simultaneously. The raincoat individual gestures toward Pug’s E.G.O. handgun — proposing a trade. Before anything is resolved, the turtleneck man — Sean — picks it up instead.
Pug claims the dark funeral suit, donning it immediately. He takes the lever-action rifle and the small cane with the black fedora, storing his samurai armor and corporate suit. Burr claims the skull mace, having activated it with his blood. Sean’s crew takes two standard uniforms, each with a handgun and baton.
With the armory looted, the group gathers their findings and heads back toward the client — the contract stipulates that the client gets first pick of the spoils.
