Summary
Kicked out of the doctor’s shop, Pug kicks a rock down the street and mutters. Then he spots a blue door, halfway open, set into a wall with no frame around it. Something tugs at him from within, as though his very blood is beckoning him forward. He steps through, into an elevator. The doors shut, the lights blink on.
He finds himself in his corporate suit, mint condition, and nothing else of his equipment. A blue armband on his arm, a lanyard hanging from his pocket with his ID within. He reads it: L CORP, Pug, L2 Management Agent, Welfare Department. The elevator dings. He steps into a familiar cafeteria — two soda machines to the right, employees gathered before them. His body moves on its own, down a corridor he has walked many times.
Three doors on his right. Large, heavy, hermetically sealed. He feels an equal draw to each. Behind the first, a spotless white kitchen, everything in its place — a swell of accomplishment, then a smudge on a plate, and a frustration that pulls him toward the door. Behind the second, a dark room, raindrops hitting the window from the inside, old wooden walls streaked with scrapes and scratches. Someone waits in there, but he cannot remember who. Behind the third, a faint hope that curdles into cold — burned wooden walls, and the knowledge that no one is left. He did not make it in time.
He opens the third door. The room has stretched and lengthened. At the far end, beside a vivid portrait of a winter landscape untouched by the fire, stands an old man in a worn grey funeral suit, a fedora on his head, wrinkled hands clasped over a cane. He does not turn. “Are you interested in hearing my stories…?” He speaks within Pug’s mind. His stories are long. They only end one way.
Pug asks him to share how they end. “Then listen well…” The old man begins to speak, his words echoing through Pug’s mind. Pug listens intently, and as he does, blood begins to drip from his nose. A red light blooms behind him as a containment door depressurizes and opens. Still the old man speaks. Blood trickles from Pug’s ears. An alarm blares in the distance. The painting behind the old man shifts — the winter landscape turning orange, flames consuming a burning house. The room heats. “Just.. this one last story, my dear boy.” Pug’s vision blurs, liquid dripping from his eyes, a pressure building in his skull. He stays to hear the final story. Everything he loved, gone. All of it, reduced to ash. He had not made it in time. The loneliness of his tale coalesces, and from his knees he collapses to the floor.

Summary
Pug collapses from his knees onto the cold asphalt of the alleyway, blood pooling from his eyes, nose, and ears. Half blind, half deaf, he wanders, unable to tell where he is going. Footsteps come up behind him — the sharp clatter of formalwear. A soft hand settles on his shoulder. “There, there.. You just need a bit of guidance, don’t you? Go along. He’s waiting for you.” Pug asks who. “Your friend. Er.. I guess you’d prefer to say acquaintance? Nonetheless, it’s where you ought to be.” The figure guides his stumbling steps, steadying him around obstacles.
Pug asks who they are and why they are helping. ”…Just someone that wants to even the scales a bit. And someone who doesn’t like to see stories end.” They tell Pug he can relax, and that they like his new look. Then they cover his eyes, and the world goes black. His body keeps moving on autopilot, a strange static flowing through him. “Good work.~”
Pug blinks his eyes open, narrowly avoiding walking into a window. He is back at the grocery store. Looking down, he finds himself clad in a burnt-out grey funeral suit — an overlay that conceals the rest of his gear beneath it. Atop his head sits a black bowler hat with a black ribbon wrapped around it. In his right hand, a long cane. He feels remarkably good — the weak, withdrawal-like feeling gone, no more trembling, no more coughing. The store is brighter to his eyes now; he can make out shapes in the darkness.
Navigating the aisles, he finds a body — head gone, organs stripped, clothing torn away, chest cavity ripped open. Beyond it, beneath the tarp where he left him, the familiar shape of Burr, limp and unmoving. Pug pokes him with the cane. Burr slowly awakens. Pug frees him, cutting away the duct tape and removing the tarp. Visually, Burr is the same as before: left arm fractured with the bone threatening to poke through, right arm bulging and bright red, chest still partially caved in, lungs whistling. Yet he moves normally. He pushes the bone back into place with a crunch. He flexes his fingers — limited movement, unable to fully form a fist, but some control returns. He prays for healing. Nothing answers.
Burr kneels over the dead Stray Dog and bites into the corpse, tearing at a chunk of flesh. It is grisly, tough, and does not taste good. He feels no different afterward, and spits it out — assumedly not a zombie. The two then set out toward the doctor who had kicked Pug out, Pug leading most of the way before showing Burr the rest.
Changes

Summary
Burr descends the steps and presses on the door marked with the blue cross. It does not open. He pushes again; it feels like pushing against a wall. He returns to Pug, prays for an answer, and gets none. Back at the door, he knocks. And keeps knocking. “What?! We’re closed!!” A muffled voice from within. Burr knocks on, bone upon metal, until the doctor calls out again.
Burr says he is heinously injured. The doctor asks how much Ahn he has, and what he is fixing. Burr gives a quick overview. “Jeeesus. You keepin’ that body, or throwin’ it out?” The doctor offers full-body prosthetics — “all ya gotta worry ‘bout is oilin’ yer brain” — but Burr insists on keeping his flesh. “Repairs of the flesh are harder than repairin’ gon’ be pricier.” The door unlatches.
Inside, the doctor sits behind a reinforced, tinted window, then presses a button that opens a door onto an operating room — gray metal, grates on the floor, closer to a dissection table than a surgical suite. Burr straps himself in, binding his legs and then his arms. The doctor eyes him and the straps, then examines him. Ribs done for, right hand “fucked up,” left looking okay, feet “too fried” to save. Burr agrees to replace his skeleton and his hands and feet. The doctor charts him up and steps into the other room. “Be back soon.”
Time passes. From the ceiling above, Burr hears rattling. A whisper from the darkness: “I am the creature of the vents, answer my riddle three and you may get out of here for free.” Burr plays along — a fan, then a cowboy whose horse is named Friday. The vent cover pops off, and Pug drops from the ceiling in a heap of black clothing and metal.
Pug frees Burr’s arm straps before the doctor walks back in and freezes at the sight of the broken vent. Negotiations resume. The doctor quotes around three hundred thousand Ahn, then knocks it down to two hundred flat if Pug pays. Pug calls him a ripper and asks to inspect the goods; the doctor shows him the implants. Pug declares it an overpriced scam and wagers two thousand Ahn that Burr will see through the “craftsmanship.” Burr looks the implants over and says no. The doctor, appalled, pays Pug the two thousand Ahn and tells them to get out — he is going for a smoke. Pug frees Burr, and the two of them walk out.

Summary
On the way back to the building where they spent the night, Pug and Burr round a street corner and find two figures by an alleyway: a hooded man grabbing the throat of a smaller figure in layered scrap clothing, pinning them to the wall. “P-Please.. I’ve given you everything I’ve got..!” Burr walks toward them. The hooded man tells him to mind his own business, shoves the woman aside, and raises his fists. Burr spots the dull gleam of a ring on the man’s right hand.
Burr tells the woman to go to Pug; she latches onto Pug’s arm. Pug introduces himself as the Vent Keeper and Burr as his zombie companion. As Burr locks onto the man, the world seems to slow for him — the fog drifting slower, his footing more grounded, his strikes more certain.
Burr dashes in with an overhead haymaker, moving faster than he ever has. The man dodges, a scrap of his hood tearing away. The man counters with a kick to Burr’s side, a purple glow flaring beneath his clothes. Burr tanks it — once, such a blow would have thrown him several meters. He grabs the man’s leg, slams a fist down on the knee, and the ring cracks, flashing white and sizzling with electricity. “SPECIAL MOVE…! RAT… THROW..!!” Burr whirls the man and hurls him into a wall, then drives a flying knee into his face. The man crumples.
Burr checks himself: the skin is gone from his knee, which clicks oddly. His side, where he was kicked, has a lower rib sticking out through the skin; he pushes it back in, feeling only pressure. He strips the man — two jackets, one hooded and blood-splattered, his pants, his wife beater tank top, an unworn chain, and the dull ring, no longer sparking. A wallet holds 3,200 Ahn, which he tosses to Pug. The woman, frozen and horrified, whispers “Monster… He’s a monster,” lets go of Pug’s arm, and runs. The two climb to their room on the 16th floor; Burr is not tired on the stairs, though his leg keeps clicking. He tries to make his scars glow. They do not. They turn in for the night.

Summary
Pug wakes with a rumbling stomach and a parched mouth. He reaches into his suit pocket, thinks of the flashlight, and withdraws it. The two descend to the street and return to the scene of the fight. The body is gone; a blood trail leads into a nearby alley.
Along the way, Pug concentrates on his suit, willing it to emit smoke. A cold longing aches in his chest — snow crunching underfoot, a lonely road. If only he had been faster. Smoke begins to billow from his cane, and its form turns into a lever-action rifle, soft smoky trails curling from the suit’s edges too. Intuitively, he understands: this loneliness can only be reprieved by sharing it — each bullet carries a message, each shot a tale, each pull of the trigger a lesson. It only ever ends one way.
The blood trail leads to a rickety door. Burr knocks — “Tis I! The zombie compatriot!” — to no reply. He kicks the door until it gives way, then follows the trail down a dark hall to a room lit from beneath a locked door. “Hello~ I think you have something that belongs to me in there.” “Who the Hell are you?! What’s this a’yer’s we got?!” Burr says he killed the man, so the body is his. “Y’left it! Finder’s keepers!” Burr kicks the door. “Fiiinal warnin’! Hope y’rember the Smoke War!”
Burr tells Pug to shoot. Pug’s rifle blasts the door open, splinters flying toward Burr. Pug fires again through the opening; a man inside yells out. Then, from within, another shot rings out, and something fleshy splatters the walls. Burr looks down: his large intestine is perforated, torn open, spilling from his lower torso, his flesh painted on the back wall. He walks forward, pushes his intestines back in, and unlocks the door before sinking to his knees.
Pug steps past him into the room. A horror scene: a crumpled body clutching a single-shot rifle; a man missing his head above the lower jaw, skull matter redecorating the room; two others clutching knives and cowering. The harvested Stray Dog lies on the floor, torso opened, filled plastic bags nearby. Pug kicks the door open and aims. One drops his knife; the other — a woman — lunges with a scalpel, and Pug shoots her in the forehead. She stumbles back, trips over the body, and lies still. The remaining man screams as Burr drags himself toward the corpse.
Then Pug hears a bell toll from Burr’s direction — a single ring, like a gong, reverberating. The remaining scavenger stops screaming, perplexed. And Pug hears the sound of rattling chains behind him.

Summary
Burr finds himself standing on a hill, pushing himself up from the grass. His corporate suit is untattered. Rolling green hills and meadows stretch to the horizon. Behind him, a great tree — massive, then shrinking into a normal tree as his eyes adjust. Beneath its shade stands a woman, her back to him: brown hair in a ponytail, a white coat, an easel before her, paintboard in one hand, brush in the other.
Burr tries to speak but finds no voice. She turns as though she heard him. He cannot make out her features — they blur, full of warmth. Behind her, the painting: the meadow in grayscale, with small splotches of color — orange over grass, red in sky, green on the sun. “Hello, my child.” She tells him they have spoken just earlier; he has been waiting a long time. “That child does depend upon you, just as much as you depend upon that child.” She says he cannot quite make up his mind — before he can paint the world in his own colors, he has doubts to handle. She sets aside her tools and points over his shoulder. On her forearms, just beneath the sleeves, he spies numerous reddened marks.
At the other end of a hill stands a coffin, wrapped in chains. When Burr turns to ask if it is him within, the woman is gone. He walks to the coffin — far too large for a man — and begins prying the chains apart. They strain, then explode at several points, the chains flying off to wrap around him. He feels unbound despite them. On the coffin lies a sword: thick, heavy, flat-tipped, double-edged — dulled and thick on one side, sharp on the other. An executioner’s blade.
Burr takes the sword and throws the coffin open. He finds himself swallowed into a dungeon — barren stone, barred windows, cobwebbed ceiling — standing in chain armor, blade in hand. Before him, in the darkness, a monstrous figure: towering, blindfolded, bandaged over a torn cheek, lightning scars across its body, chains trailing from its wrists and waist. Its arms blend into metal slabs — masses of raw iron, far too big to be called swords.
“Ah. So you’re me, and I’m you.” Burr speaks. “I can free you.” The creature grins, a maddening bloodlust in the air. “You’re a manifestation of a part of me that craves violence.” The creature roars and charges.

Summary
Pug turns toward the noise from the direction of his dying companion. Burr is staggering upright, covered and bound in chains that spill from his side, a few links “stitching” his wound shut. A blindfold, loosely wrapped, covers his eyes. His right arm has formed into a long blade reaching the floor from his elbow — thick, heavy, double-sided, dull on one edge, glistening sharp on the other. Chains wrap the blade up to midway.
Burr leans forward, animalistic, and dashes at Pug, blade raised, sparks grinding. Pug steps aside — no need to redirect — and Burr leaps past, cleaving through the metal bedframe the remaining organ harvester huddled against, through the harvester’s head, and through the wall. Wood, bone, and metal shatter and splinter.
Burr turns back to Pug and charges again, the blade crashing into the floorboards and down through the head of the comatose organ harvester, bisecting them before stopping in the floor. Pug runs for the window, leaps over a kitchen counter, and throws himself out. He rolls, keeps moving, and runs. Behind him, furniture and glass shatter, then a door crunches and explodes outward thirty feet back.
Pug reaches a street where scavengers are looting a store. “Oooii! ‘o th’ell’re y’?!” “Whatever you do, don’t look that way!” Pug yells, running past. A single swing cleaves through three men — the first two killed instantly, the third’s legs split — as Burr continues the chase.
Pug turns, skids, aims the lever-action rifle, and fires three shots. Burr swings: he cuts through the first bullet; the second strikes the blade’s dull edge; the third strikes his shin, and he topples, tumbling before stopping himself by tearing into the asphalt. Pug runs, glancing back to watch Burr stand.

Summary
Burr swings upward at his monstrous self, lamenting its lack of form and fighting knowledge. The creature’s blade crashes into the ground, tearing up brick and rubble. It pivots on its blade, terrifyingly graceful, and swings for Burr’s center. Burr blocks, but the blow sends him flying into a pillar.
He stands, drops his sword, and faces the monster. “I won’t fight you. I accept you. I accept this part of myself.” The creature charges, arm raised to cleave. Burr steps in, arms open, refusing to fight, choosing instead to embrace that part of himself.
“And so, the Child stepped forward, his arms splayed open, and refusing to fight his monster, and instead, choosing to accept that part of himself.” A voice narrates. “That’s a different ending, don’t you think?”
Outside the barred window, three comets streak across the night sky toward the cell. The first explodes into two, fizzling away. The second strikes a stone tower, shaking the dungeon. The third shatters through the window and flies into the monster’s leg, which shatters — dematerializing into black miasma. The creature’s lunge falters; it crashes beside the pillar, within reach.
Burr steps forward and embraces himself, removing the blindfold. His chain armor unwinds, latching onto the monster and wrapping around its sword arms. He loosens and undoes the blindfold until, at last, he reveals one eye — and from within it shines the warmth of sunlight. “An.. unexpected Choice. This Child truly does need the other. Perhaps… Perhaps I was wrong. But there will be another time to reflect. For now… I can’t wait to see what Colors you Children bring to this City.”

Summary
The two of them set out for the primary base of Bosco’s pack with no lead worth following, so they take the streets instead, looking for former Stray Dogs to interrogate. Burr catches blood on the air and follows it through the winding Backstreets until the clash of metal resolves into a parking lot. A dozen scavengers hang back with baseball bats, tire irons and knives, watching three of their own fight barehanded. What those three have cornered are three figures in dress shirts: one with a black-bladed longsword and his black hair tied up into a small ponytail, one with his sleeves rolled back fighting with a tonfa baton and a mace, and a third cowering behind a car clutching two bags with a flatcap pulled down over their face.
Burr marches in with his sword arm grinding the asphalt and his chains clattering behind him, and the fight stops as the whole lot turn to look at him, and at Pug leaning against a wall with black miasma bleeding off him. He asks who belongs to the Stray Dogs. One of the fighters answers that they ran with them until last week, and at Burr’s gesture two thirds of the crowd splits off into the streets. Four stay frozen where they are, and the one who spoke bargains: there is a place nearby, two or three dozen of them in it, and he knows a couple of names of the other packs though not where they were deployed. Burr tells him he will lead them there. The flatcap turns out to belong to a small woman who asks whether she is free to go, and she is.
Then Burr asks the man how many innocent people he has killed. The question lands as nonsense. A boss says kill and you kill, he answers, and it makes no difference whose orders anyone was following. Burr slashes and the man throws himself backwards on a purple glow with his forearm raised, his sleeve destroyed and the bruised, tattooed skin beneath it smoking. Burr presses him, calls him a stray dog who only follows orders, and the man answers that if it is his time to be put down then that is that, and that there is no meaning in any of their deaths.
Burr lunges. The man sidesteps, kicks him in the side hard enough to pop chainlinks, and keeps arguing. Burr swings again, forcing the blade through the chains’ resistance until some of them snap, and the blow breaks both of the man’s arms and throws him into a car.
Burr tells Pug to watch the others and walks to the car. The second man moves, and Pug is already tracking him from across the street. The first shot takes him in the chest. Two more follow as he staggers upright, and by then blood is running from his nose, his eyes and his ears. He says it is too late, punches through the car window, and drives his own neck down onto the jagged glass. He dies quietly, looking into some distant plane.
The last of them is left on the ground. The man against the car meets Burr with a knowing nod, as though he prefers this to the alternative, and Burr puts the blade through his chest, grinding through the ribcage while the chains fight him the whole way and another link snaps off the blade.
Pug concentrates on his rifle and runs it down through a revolver and a failed attempt at a rocket launcher until it settles back into the cane. The one who can still walk leads them out, insisting he only killed a few to protect himself. Burr tells him he can go and turns his back. What waits ahead is the apartment complex the guerilla fighters sent them to, and when they tell the man at the door to take them to their boss, he looks at the two of them and does as he is told.

Summary
The door swings shut behind them and the room resolves into a processing floor. Tables shoved together make a counter, a second guard sits behind it with a long firearm across his knees and a bottle frozen halfway to his mouth, and past him a queue of locals in bundled rags wait with papers in their hands to be seen at the old reception desk. Burr tells the doorman to keep going. They pass through the line, and the only one who holds their gaze is a boy of about fifteen in a coat several sizes too large with a kitchen knife pushed through his belt. Burr tells him to go home, and an older woman wraps her arms around the boy, covers his eyes, bows an apology without meeting theirs, and pulls him back into the queue.
Upstairs the air turns warm and humid against the chill outside. Laundry hangs across the corridor, faces glance at them and disappear, and doors shut one by one ahead of them. The hallway opens into a common room where a card game stops dead, weapons and a few firearms laid out within reach and nobody reaching for them. Burr asks who the boss is. A girl’s voice from a door says Lupo. The man who startles up from the table is in his late thirties, shares her resemblance, and tells them Lupo is upstairs on a higher floor.
The third floor smells of oil and grease, its interior walls knocked through into rows of bunks and a mess hall. These men are harder, cliques of them with machetes and hatchets, one sharpening a cleaver with arms cased in an industrial exo-frame built for hauling crates. One has a metal hand emerging from layered rags. The two of them help themselves to the pot of soup slop, a dark brown mixture of broth, potted meat and ground meat, while a man in yellow goggles and a KISS THE CH<3F apron backs away. They pass a door marked ARMORY.
The fourth floor is a hangout of blacked-out curtains, floodlights and tarps, crates stamped D22, a radio playing EDM and a Stray Dog having his tattoos tuned. The tuner says District 22 and tells them Bosco is finished, that whatever orders they carry are kaput, and to go talk to Sal. Burr notices the tattoos on these men are faded, some of them closer to scars, and that they scratch at them when they think no one is looking. The doorman points them at the fifth floor and holds out his hands for the trays. Pug tips him a hundred Ahn, the man pockets it without a word, and Burr calls Pug a cheap-ass on the way up.
On the fifth floor a guard in a white collared shirt with tattooed forearms welcomes them in and goes to fetch Sal. Big Sal arrives stocky, in a wife beater and leather jacket, and explains that Bosco’s death is done business, that the Pound was between Bosco and the Handler, and that they are not Stray Dogs any longer because Signore Lupo holds the leash. He goes to ask whether Lupo will see them. The guard who returns to escort them chats on the way, asks where Pug got his suit, says looking at it fills him with a sense of loneliness, and asks whether they have met before. He gives his name as Jude.
Lupo sits cross-legged on the floor in a plain white T-shirt, lean and tattooed, undecorated. Big Sal sits on a couch in a chain necklace beside a Stray Dog wearing sunglasses indoors and heavy rings. Three scavengers wait to one side, one in a puffy black-camouflage jacket with a cloth half-mask, one in a skull balaclava and aviators, one in a black balaclava with a beanie. Burr gives the account of Bosco’s death: four men, one killed and two injured, Bosco shot down, a swordsman ending the fight, all of it starting from a breakout Bosco let happen by not minding his duties. Lupo accepts it and says Bosco was a piece of shit who stranded them out here with no connection back to the Handler.
Then Burr says the two of them were among the reasons Bosco died. The room goes quiet. Burr leans on his sword arm, looks at every face in it, and says that it happens. Lupo asks him to explain, and Burr does, from the top of the Pound to the escape, to Bosco’s arrival, to the swordsman letting them walk. Veins stand out on Big Sal’s face. Lupo simply nods and asks what their business is now, and Burr says his original business was to wipe out the Stray Dogs and that he does not know what to do with it now.
Lupo sets the record. It has been a week, nobody has come to reconnect them, and they understand themselves to have been left for dead. They have taken what they needed to survive, and those who want to survive come to them for shelter, which is what the queue downstairs is. Burr says that is what confused him, and says they look like they could turn back into bad men the moment someone comes to collect them. Lupo answers that nobody is coming, that the initiative was a death sentence and there is no way home.
Then Burr starts to ramble to himself about what is right and what is wrong, and the chains on his sword begin to shift and snap at their bindings. The room looks around in confusion except Lupo, who only watches. Burr asks whether men who start doing good make themselves good or merely circumstantial heroes, and asks what is so impressive about surviving. A bell tolls somewhere distant, like a gong.
Lupo answers that he never stopped to think about good or bad, that neither did his men, that it was the Stray Dogs or death and the expedition or death, and that survival never had anything to do with either. Burr tells him good and evil has everything to do with it, and speaks of why She told him to paint the world, that the whole thing needs redoing. A second bell tolls. He says everyone is frightened and uses it as an excuse for heinous things, and the links of his chains begin to snap one by one.
The blade’s edge sharpens and the blindfold widens until it covers both eyes. Burr says he hates this world, says he will fix it, laughs, and Pug brings his cane down at the back of his head as the third bell tolls. A wall of force erupts and throws Pug, the cane and Jude back across the room.
One of the scavengers shouts fire and the man in the puffy hood unslings a rifle and pulls the trigger. The round crosses the room and simply stops in the air, then drops to the floor. Lupo and his men are already up with their tattoos lit. Burr tells the air that he understands and that the world needs repainting, then says that wanting to survive does not excuse the innocent dead, and that if survival is the excuse for doing wrong then the one who does it does not deserve to survive.
A blinding warm light comes off him, the chains rattle and creak and finally let go, and the weighted links fall to the floor. What stands there is the Sin of Survival, the Unbound Executioner, both arms out and shaped into swords, the blindfold wound tight around the head until there is nothing beneath it that could be called eye sockets.
Its first swing sweeps the length of the room. Pug ducks under it as it tears through desks, walls and bodies. When it ends, the Stray Dogs have all evaded it, Big Sal has lost an arm, and two of the three scavengers have been bisected while the rifleman went out the window to whatever waited five floors down. Jude has dived flat.
Big Sal stays back while Lupo and the sunglassed Stray Dog drive in, their strikes landing on the blades he uses as shields. Pug turns the cane into a revolver and fans the hammer four times, three of them striking as the Stray Dogs push the blades aside to open him up, and the fourth going wide. Above Burr’s head three black lines appear, then a fourth, then a fifth drawn across them all. Pug’s revolver clicks empty and shifts into a hunting pistol with a barrel glowing like heated embers.
The Executioner throws itself at Pug in an all-or-nothing charge and kicks him square in the chest as the trigger is pulled. Behind it, a figure larger than Burr stands with its arms over its face, and says it is not too late this time, and that this story will be different. The pistol flares, discharging everything it holds in one blast, and the five tallies light into flame. The creature rockets backwards out through the window, taking chunks of wall with it, burning as it goes.
Pug’s body follows the kick backwards through the door, tumbling across the fifth floor, and down the stairs. The world goes black.

lore/strike-face.title: Strike-Face
lore/strike-face.content:
Strike-Face
Origin
Before the Corps perfected kinetic-energy manipulation, the technology began as a simple ceramic trauma plate manufactured by an early, defunct iteration of what was then K Corp — not to be confused with the present-day K Corp, which produces the Heliapoeisis healing drug and has no connection to kinetic-energy technology. The plates were stamped with a directional arrow and two words on the strike side: “STRIKE ← FACE” — telling the wearer which side took the bullet. Soldiers in the field began calling them “Strike-Face plates,” then simply “Strike-Faces.” The name outlasted the plate.
As Former K Corp refined its understanding of kinetic energy — absorption, redirection, dissipation — the technology miniaturized. The ceramic plate was no longer the vessel; the principle could be embedded into rings, chains, fabric, even tattoos. But the linguistic split was already complete.
The Split
At some point in the late corporate era, R&D formally divided the product line:























BranchDomainClean NameDegraded (Backstreets)StrikeOffensive — amplifying, directing, or delivering kinetic forceStrike Gear → StrikewearStrykewer → StrykeFaceDefensive — absorbing, dispersing, or nullifying incoming kinetic forceFace Gear → FacewearFaysewer → Fayse
The original plates became obsolete as a corporate product but never disappeared. They were too reliable to abandon.
Operational Tiers
Modern Strike-Face accessories fall into three functional categories per branch, regardless of form factor.
Fayses — Electrical Management
Defensive accessories themed around electrical circuit management: current, threshold, and load.
Fuse
Sacrificial. Single-impact. Destroyed on activation.
A Fuse detects incoming kinetic energy above a calibrated threshold, absorbs the full force, and shatters irreversibly. The wearer takes nothing. The accessory is gone.

Analogue: ceramic trauma plate
Cost: cheap, disposable, easily scavenged
Common forms: rings, thin chains, single-use plates

Breaker
Trips and resets. Absorbs a hit, goes dormant, repairable.
A Breaker thresholds similarly to a Fuse, but rather than destroying itself, it trips — dumping the energy and entering a cooldown state. It must be manually reset, repaired, or allowed to recharge before the next activation. While dormant, it offers no protection.

Analogue: steel plate — takes several rounds, then needs reworking
Cost: mid-tier, requires a Tuner or workshop for maintenance
Common forms: heavier chains, reinforced bracers, plate carriers with reset switches

Buffer
Always active. Dampens impact. Near-indestructible.
A Buffer does not wait for a threshold. It is a persistent kinetic dampener — absorptive material that bleeds force out of every impact. It lets damage through; it merely ensures the damage is never fatal in a single strike. Buffers are the most durable tier, and the most expensive.

Analogue: UHMWPE polymer plate — catches round after round, never shatters, eventually needs replacement
Cost: expensive, specialist
Common forms: suit-integrated linings, vest inserts, high-end bracers

Strykes — Thermal Management
Offensive accessories themed around industrial thermal control: heat buildup, venting, and dissipation. These are not fire — they are heat exchangers.
Flash
Unregulated thermal dump. Single-strike burnout.
A Flash converts stored kinetic potential into raw force with no thermal regulation — maximum amplification, all heat vented in one strike. Overheats the accessory, burns the user, and often destroys itself. The spectacle is the point.

Analogue: ceramic plate shattering on impact
Cost: cheap, dramatic, easy to scavenge but dangerous to use
Common forms: rings (Burr’s overheated bronze ring), single-use knuckles
Favored by: Stray Dogs — every punch is a statement

Flare
Thermal spike with cooldown cycle. Burst-fire.
A Flare delivers force in discrete thermal spikes, then cycles down to shed heat before the next activation. Hits hard, but the gap between bursts leaves the user vulnerable. More controlled than a Flash, still visibly aggressive.

Analogue: a temperature spike on a monitoring graph — sharp rise, sharp fall
Cost: mid-tier, requires venting period or external cooling between cycles
Common forms: heavier rings, gauntlet inserts, paired accessories for staggered cycling

Sink
Continuous heat dissipation. Always on. Never overheats.
A Sink converts kinetic force to thermal energy and disperses it steadily across its surface — no spikes, no venting, no burnout. It does not amplify as aggressively as a Flash or Flare, but it never hurts the user, never quits, and never needs cycling. A Fixer’s choice.

Analogue: heatsink — constant thermal load, constant dissipation
Cost: expensive, specialist, requires precision engineering
Common forms: suit-integrated panels, gauntlet plates, professional-grade rings
Favored by: Fixers — a working arm is worth more than a spectacular punch

Generational Layering






























TierWhat They WearWhoOriginalActual Strike-Face ceramic plates, legacy carriersWar veterans, old-timers, traditionalists. No fancy failure modes.StreetStrykes and Fayses in scavenged form factors — stolen rings, jury-rigged chainsScavengers, low-rank gang members. Whatever could be looted.ProfessionalPlate carriers with embedded Fayses; suit-integrated StrykesFixers, Syndicate enforcers, security contractors. The plate still catches the round when the tech fails.FactionSame tech, factional housingStray Dogs use chains and rings for visibility; Syndicate weaves it into tailored suits; zealots tattoo circuits directly into skin.
The plate carrier’s persistence at the professional tier is not nostalgia. It is pragmatism. When the kinetic layer fails — when the Fuse shatters or the Breaker trips — there is still dumb ceramic underneath. In The City, redundancy is not a luxury.
Vernacular
Modern Backstreets speech has long abandoned “Strike Gear” and “Face Gear”:

“He’s running double Fayses” — two defensive accessories stacked.
“That punch had a Stryke behind it” — offensive kinetic assist.
“Fayse popped” / “Fayse is down” — a Fuse or Breaker just triggered.
“Old man’s still wearing plates — swear to god, a Strykeface carrier from the war” — an antique, the technology in its original form factor.
“Needs a re-Fayse” — needs a replacement defensive accessory.
“He’s Flash-fried his arm” — overheated a Stryke and burned himself.
“Running hot” — a Flare mid-cycle, or a Sink approaching its thermal limit.

reference/faust-warp-train-dialogue.content:
Faust Dialogue — Murder on the WARP Express (Intervallo IV)
Year: 984-11 | Episodes 1-14


Dante, please respond. There’s—


Dante, I understand your considerable degree of disorientation, but—


Your alarmed response and possible incompliance have already been accounted for.


Faust has indeed known this all along, as no knowledge is out of Faust’s reach. As expected, a solution to your dilemma has already been prepared.


The rearmost tail cars of WARP trains are all freight cars. That is where Mephistopheles will be safely fastened and transported.


And the LCB will…


… have the benefit of boarding as first class passengers.


The company’s budget is not a subject that warrants your concern.


That is the promotional language, yes. They are flash-freeze hibernation capsules, to be precise.


They have been designed to easily withstand the ‘true’ amount of time it takes for the WARP train to travel from point A to point B. The trip will be over in the blink of an eye for the passengers.


… Yes.


Dante, let us proceed this way.


Please elaborate on your exact definition of ‘safe’.


A flash-freeze hibernation device will put you in a temporary state of death caused by rapid cellular cryopreservation process. However, the rapidity of the process prevents damage to your cells during the phase change. Therefore, in most normal cases, this will not cause any issues.


Faust is aware that this model has fully resolved cell membrane-breaching issues caused by cryogenic density change or by ice crystal growths of hydrogen molecules.


Yes, as far as Faust is aware. Even if an issue were to arise during the journey, because everyone will be reverted to their states at the beginning of the train trip upon arrival, there won’t be any lasting complications from the said problem.


Indeed. As Faust’s talents are not limited to a singular field.


As a general rule, Faust does not err. However, Faust is also not a divine being.


There are certain information in the world that Faust is yet to have access to. Therefore, while Faust may speak the facts, what is said may not always align with the truth.


In order to prevent cases of unnecessary anxiety and misgivings among the Sinners, the history of accidents that has occurred aboard WARP trains will not be shared.


Then, let us hurry and enter our capsules before it is too late.


Is it anxiety, Dante?


Allow me to assist you. Stand as though you are leaning back, and…


Do not worry too much.


… We will meet again in but a moment, Dante.


Dante, you must wake up. Dante—


… An inconceivable situation has occurred.


No, we are not yet at our destination.


Yes.


… I believe we are currently stranded in an unidentified dimension. Coordinates: unknown.


………….


You are half correct, yet half incorrect.


Dante. I understand your confusion, however… perhaps an elaboration of our present circumstance is necessary.


Thank you. Then…


The Distortions themselves likely did not pose a problem for W Corp. Based on the available information, it can be determined that they would have all been neutralized as soon as the train arrived, and any transformed passengers would have been reverted to their human forms.


But…


That is the question for which we must discover the precise cause and effect of.


… That appears to be the most prominent cause of this misunderstanding.


However, we were given this master keycard that can open and close the hibernation capsules at will.


We may return to our respective capsules as soon as the contract is fulfilled and safely complete the rest of the journey as we had planned from the beginning.


That is…


… Next time, I will take your inputs into account.


… That, is something I must first discuss with Dante.


We must converse in a lower volume, Dante.


… My connection to Gesellschaft… I mean, Faust, has been severed.


I… cannot access Faust’s knowledge at the moment.


I mean it in the most literal sense. My access to Faust’s input and information, which has always been readily available… is completely severed.


One cannot completely dismiss that possibility, but even that is… uncertain…


Yes. At this moment, I am… limited to operating only with my knowledge.


I cannot discern the cause of this disconnection… More than enough precautions have likely been taken in case of interdimensional travel, but perhaps Faust did not take into account an occasion in which we may have to access an unidentified dimension such as this. Or, even if it was taken into account, this particular dimension may not yet have been subject to cross-observation.


If that is not the case, then I-no, nevermind.


There was nothing that suggested that my connection to Faust would be lost, not even as we boarded the train. To be honest, this is…


… a rather disagreeable situation for me.


… Understood.


And… to the Sinners…


… the fact that we are currently confined to a WARP train in operation must be a source of enough stress. I believe that sharing Faust’s current state with them would add an unnecessary source of tension.


In the grand scheme of things, yes.


By A Corp.’s standard time scale, approximately three days have passed since our departure.


As per the contract between Limbus Company and W Corp., I acquired the master keycard placed inside my capsule and adjusted the hatch settings to open automatically in three days.


As you were all informed prior to boarding, there is no way for the economy class passengers to enter the first class car; that is why this place has remained untouched.


However, cross-referencing my own deductions and W Corp.’s rather fragmentary explanations, I can assume that ‘the situation’ is currently under progress in the economy class cars.


Precisely. In my opinion, it is—


Please step aside for a moment, Don Quixote. It would be best if I observed it with my own eyes.


I intend to follow your usual flavor of suggestion, Heathcliff.


That there are times in which a physical altercation is preferable to detached ruminations.


After all… how could I deduce anything without seeing it myself?


… Don Quixote.


They are not dead.


Observe closer. The parts are all tethered to one another by something, are they not?


It appears that the flow of time has ceased in this space. Therefore, it follows that the… connections, that tether bodies to life and away from death, remain intact.


Yes. That is a most rational suggestion, Yi Sang.


If their severed parts are all connected… then it can be said that no matter how entangled their bodies become, it is not impossible to eventually gather their parts together to form a single passenger.


Thus, naturally, we can determine how and why the profession ‘W Corp. Cleanup Agent’ has come to be.


Dante.


… Indeed. I intend to collect further intelligence.


Are they Distortions, or… Abnormalities?


Is it difficult to be certain at the moment?


Faust may know… but I, at this moment, have no way of knowing.


There is no need, Dante.


Though the information you have provided me is rather ambiguous, it has helped me deduce something of worth.


And…


Collecting intelligence myself and creating deductions based on sparse information is quite…


… She appeared without warning.


Have you not left this car for the duration of the ride, Sasha?


Hasn’t something else of note also occurred?


… You have decided to protect them, despite the potential risk that they may transform as well.


… I see.


W Corp. has hired us to solve this case. We are…


Um…


Indeed… Fixers.


As you must be well aware yourself, contracts and contract fulfillment are of paramount importance for Fixers.


With that in mind, please recall that W Corp. is one of the most secretive Wings of the City.


This is the master keycard given to us by W Corp. I believe that it can open most doors aboard this train.


It is fortunate that someone like yourself is aboard the train. Your presence ensured that child’s survival.


Be like… what?


Eyes…


I have one last thing to inquire.


… That is quite an unsound decision to make for someone who claims to be ‘in the same line of work’ as us.


Have you considered the possibility that, once our contract is successfully completed, we could include references to a particularly cooperative Associate Office in our report to W Corp?


Were the eyes of the monsters you faced red, by any chance?


No, well.


It was a question of no significance.


Those entities are…


… What do you think those entities are?


Yes, and? Was there anything else?


Thank you, all. Your input has all been very helpful.


We are in luck, Dante.


I have read upon this subject as a tangent while perusing information regarding our next destination, moments before we boarded the train. And while that will be a useful element in resolving this situation…


… the Sinners have also been a very good source of intelligence when it came to categorizing and identifying important evidence from the available sea of information. Your advice was correct, Dante.


Nothing can be said with absolute certainty at the moment. However, this will be a good place for us to start.


… I will now present before you a solution to this predicament.


That will not change, no. However, what I am about to share will give you a better understanding of the purpose behind W Corp.’s contract, and provide us with the possible means of finding the method by which we may complete it.


It is very likely that the entity behind the incidents on this train, and by extension, every incident of the same nature that has occurred in previous WARP train trips…


… is a Bloodfiend.


… Yes. I see that some Sinners may have encountered Bloodfiends in the past. A long-winded explanation seems unnecessary.


As many of you have stated thus far, the entities we faced in this train do not appear to be ‘Bloodfiends’.


In a sense, they are dreg-like beings that have failed to become Kindreds… they are referred to as ‘Bloodbags’ among relevant parties, according to information I am aware of.


As it has been said prior, it is impossible for passengers to disappear aboard WARP trains under normal circumstances.


Though our reserve of intelligence regarding the WARP trains or W Corp. is vast, if incomplete, we could not find a possible exception to the above rule.


Within that reserve of intelligence, however, I have discovered that inserting a previously unseen variable into the equation allows for a formulation of a new hypothesis.


A more accurate descriptor would be to say that they are either dissolved or vaporized.


No matter the degree of violence the passengers may indulge in, no matter how severe the damages may be, the WARP trains can revert them to their initial states at the beginning of the journey.


Among several interpretations of the word ‘violence’ involves cannibalization, of course.


However, as the passengers’ collective time itself is in moratorium for the duration of the train’s operation, digestion is not a biological process that should be active. In other words, even the devoured passengers could be reconstructed.


However, such is not true for ‘Bloodbags’. Bloodbags are, by their nature, obsessed with blood; their existence hinges on supplying themselves with the blood of their victims.


And it is said that they must consume a minuscule amount of blood to maintain their forms.


If I were to continue my deductions… perhaps ‘consumption of blood’, for Bloodfiends and Bloodbags is a fundamentally different process from our ‘consumption of nutrients’ for energy.


To them, blood is a culmination, an entailment of something that forms the self, including but not limited to: emotions, ambitions, wealth, purposes of existence… Then, it must naturally follow that they can spend their blood at will, which is a process that is isolated from other biological processes such as digestion.


… That information is inaccessible at the moment.


This is only a speculation, however… I assume that a form of direct physical contact is needed to turn an individual into a Bloodbag. If such were not the case, then we, who are likely the greatest obstacles to this entity’s goal at the moment, would have been the first ones to be turned.


Indeed. If we are to believe the words of the Fixer from earlier, then there is a high likelihood that the horde is advancing in this direction from the back of the train…


In other words, continuing down the train cars will lead us straight to the Bloodfiend.


… Dante.


My apologies. The access to that information is prohibited at this moment as well.


… I may have been too reliant on Faust. In too many places.


He has departed the scene.


I see. There are multiple possible interpretations depending on one’s perspective, despite the fact that there is but a single scene. I will remember both of your inputs.


Yes, well. Good for them.


I am physically unharmed, yet… Hm. Yes, I am alright.


However, I do not enjoy this circumstance which we find ourselves in. It is as though I am casting nets to nowhere while lost and isolated in a blind sea.


… I could usually complete these deductions within moments after establishing a few basic cross-references between the accessible information.


… Is that so.


Although this is not common knowledge, there is a subcategory of Fixers called Bloodfiend Hunters who specialize in… yes, hunting Bloodfiends.


Assuming that information is true, it can be inferred that Bloodfiends are difficult foes that require a certain expertise to defeat.


He… must be the Bloodfiend who caused this outbreak. He is our target.


Do not let your guard down, Heathcliff. This entity has managed to turn countless passengers of this train into his Bloodbags.


This is rather curious.


It appears that this Bloodfiend leaves this car only on rare occasions…


… Yet we have seen signs of his insidious influence throughout every car we have visited so far.


Bloodfiends…


… What if there was more than a single Bloodfiend on board, one still capable of rational thought…


Don Quixote, watch out!


Kindred…


Are you even aware of the exact nature of a ‘Kindred’?


I see. A Bloodfiend’s Kindred is like a sub-entity of the Bloodfiend, similar in concept to sub-entities created by Distortions or Abnormalities.


It must have been desperation that drove you to accept that proposition without hesitation, despite the lack of relevant information.


… It appears that he has empowered himself by reaping their blood.


Don Quixote! Stop her, now!


Dante…


I believed myself to be trying my utmost to overcome this adversity…


… without access to Faust’s knowledge and intelligence.


However…


With our loss of the Master Keycard… the uncertainty of this circumstance has greatly exacerbated.


At the origin of this plight…


… must be my overreliance on Faust.


Indeed, among many, I am a Faust that believes in uncertainty.


Our loss of the master keycard is but one of innumerable uncertain variables in the equation.


The constant is, however…


… that the Bloodfiend is just as desperate as we are.


Thus the only option that remains at present is to… compromise.


Very well. Then… Cassetti, why don’t we move this conversation to a different location?


Only I will accompany Dante to this negotiation. I will make my intentions clear now: Dante and I will not attack you there.


Yes. The freight car is immediately adjacent to this one; that is where we will further discuss what we each have to offer to one another.


Correct.


Dante… this will be my first attempt…


… at a ‘gamble’.


The connection has been restored.


Boarding Mephistopheles has… reestablished my connection to Faust.


No. And as I have stated before, this was a pure, incalculable gamble based on my own uncertain hypothesis.


This success helps me somewhat comprehend Miss Rodya’s fascination with gambling.


Now that the connection has been reestablished, I would like to make a complaint against the Fausts in the Gesellschaft management regarding the fact that they neglected to list the information pertaining to the loss of connection within the interiors of the WARP trains, however…


… finding a solution to this situation takes precedence. I have much reason to believe that their omission was done on purpose, but… I hope such is not the case.


… Let us discuss the details of our compromise. What are you willing to accept in return for the master keycard?


Like nothing happened…


Our memories and any signs of battle will be entirely erased upon our arrival. We will have no way to relay our news, whether one of success or failure.


If we had the means to defeat him, then at least W Corp. would inform us that our contract was successful after the fact. However…


… this current scenario will leave us with nothing to show for, not even the smallest hint, and the contract will end in failure.


However, what takes precedence over the contract is you and the Sinners’ psychological stability.


Certainly, you are aware that your suggestion is no solution at all, Don Quixote.


… Oh, I did not expect this to be the solution…


… According to this information I had viewed in the past, and once again just now, it’s…


Mm. … Dante. Take cover behind me and remain absolutely still.


And please, do note that the other Sinners must never hear a word of what is about to happ—


She appears to be in a state of deep slumber. As she is not at a risk of death, she will be waking up soon.


The master keycard is not an absolutely necessary element to resolving this situation.


It will require approximately five hours to formulate and proceed with an explanation in a manner that will allow the Sinners to fully comprehend the exact ‘how’ of this methodology. Therefore, it will be delivered to you in a digestible, summarized format.


We can utilize the Backdoor of Mephistopheles.


To put it simply, we will spend the time at a space disconnected from the train.


The train should be arriving at its destination in approximately ten seconds, going by the A Corp. time scale. All we must do is to remain somewhere in our original dimension for that duration.


Yes. This is the correct door. Its safety is completely ensured.


I… did not bother verifying that particular information myself.


It is necessary for future endeavors that I gain the experience… of encountering something completely unexpected.


Now, please enter through this door.


5… 4… 3… 2… 1…


We are employees of Limbus Company. We boarded the WARP train at the behest of your employer.


Yes, we must have suffered from a momentary, collective hallucination caused by fatigue. Very well, then. We will see ourselves out.


Understood. Any and all relevant reports will be sent to W Corp. via LCCA, and…


Because it was the preferable course of action to having the same explosive demise occur to your body instead.


I do find it regrettable that you were made to turn the clock despite my knowledge of the high likelihood of my death upon that occurrence.


… That is something I have been aware of since the LCB was first established. The same could be said of Vergilius.


However, it was by the will of the LCA’s superiors that this knowledge remains withheld from the Manager until the appropriate moment.


… According to my private judgment, yes.


Well, as my connection to all communications, including one to Faust, had been severed. I was not in a position to receive the headquarters’ authorization for that action.
